quote: Causality is the reasonable, the law-bound, the describable, the badge of our whole waking and reasoning existence. But destiny is the word for an inner certainty that is not describable. We bring out that which is in the causal by means of a physical or an epistemological system, through numbers, by reasoned classification; but the idea of destiny can be imparted only by the artist working through media like portraiture, tragedy and music. The one requires us to distinguish and in distinguishing to dissect and destroy, whereas the other is creative through and through, and thus destiny is related to life and causality to death. In the Destiny-idea the soul reveals its world-longing, its desire to rise into the light, to accomplish and actualize its vocation. To no man is it entirely alien, and not before one has become the unanchored "late" man of the megalopolis is original vision quite overpowered by matter-of-fact feeling and mechanizing thought. Even then, in some intense hour, the lost vision comes back to one with terrible clearness, shattering in a moment all the causality of the world's surface.
author: Oswald Spengler
work: The Decline of the West, vol. 1, trans. Charles Francis Atkinson
expansion: Spengler separates two necessities and refuses to let one explain the other. Causality is the badge of waking, reasoning life: law-bound, describable, built out of distinctions, numbers, and classes. To distinguish, he says, is already to dissect and to destroy. Destiny is an inner certainty that cannot be put in that form at all. It can be imparted by portrait, tragedy, and music, the arts that show a life without taking it apart. So destiny stands to life as causality stands to death. In the idea of destiny the soul shows its world-longing, the wish to rise into the light and actualize a vocation. The late man of the megalopolis, unanchored, loses that vision to matter-of-fact feeling and mechanizing thought. Even then, in some intense hour, the vision returns and shatters the causal surface of the world.

The distinction is Spengler's deepest methodological claim, and it is aimed at the whole modern habit of explaining history by laws. Kant, on his reading, could describe the necessity that governs thinking consciousness. He could not touch the necessity of a life, and so destiny drops out of every rational system, passed over in silence because abstractions cannot hold it. Goethe is again the master: the man who lets the become be felt in its becoming, who reads a face or an epoch physiognomically. Nietzsche had already opposed life to the Socratic demand for reasons. Spengler gives that opposition a morphology. A culture's science is real, and it is late. Causality is what a soul produces when it has become civilized enough to take its own waking consciousness as the whole of truth. Portrait, tragedy, and music remain the languages in which destiny can still be shown, which is why he ranks them with religion and against the monograph.

Mechanizing thought is no longer a prophecy in the passage. It is the ordinary weather of planning, metrics, and risk. Spengler's intense hour, when the lost vision returns and the causal net tears, is the experience people still have in grief, in music, in a face, and then apologize for, as if it were a mood interrupting the real analysis. The passage says the apology is the late habit. Destiny was the original certainty, and the system of causes is a magnificent, deadly instrument laid over it. For a mind drawn to Spengler, to Goethe, and to the sense that history is heavy with fate, this is the page that earns the rest of the book. A future you can only calculate is a future from which the living part has already been subtracted.

The arts he trusts are not a miscellaneous list. Portrait, tragedy, and music are the arts Schopenhauer had already set nearest the will and the Ideas, and nearest a knowledge that is not conceptual. Spengler takes that aesthetic ranking and makes it a historical method. Where causality can be written, destiny can only be shown. The intense hour in which the late man of the megalopolis recovers the vision and the causal surface tears is his secular sublime: Burke's terror and Schopenhauer's exaltation, relocated from the cliff and the storm to a moment inside a civilization that has forgotten fate. Charles Taylor, decades later, describes the buffered self and the immanent frame as the felt shape of a life for which meanings no longer cross the boundary of the mind. He does not prophesy the death of the West. He describes the same late consciousness from the inside, as a historical achievement that exacts a price.

Goethe remains the master Spengler claims, and the claim is specific. Morphology, learned on plants and on color, is the art of letting a form show its life without dissecting it into causes. Applied to cultures, it yields destiny as physiognomy. The danger of the method is that a physiognomy can become a stereotype with a timetable. The justification of the method is the experience the passage ends on, which people still have and then apologize for: grief, a face, a piece of music, an hour in which the net of causes is obviously not the whole. The apology is what he calls the late habit.

quote: Must the morning always return? Will the despotism of the earthly never cease? Unholy activity consumes the angel-visit of the Night. Will the time never come when Love's hidden sacrifice shall burn eternally? To the Light a season was set; but everlasting and boundless is the dominion of the Night. Endless is the duration of sleep. Holy Sleep, gladden not too seldom in this earthly day-labour, the devoted servant of the Night. Fools alone mistake thee, knowing nought of sleep but the shadow which, in the gloaming of the real night, thou pitifully castest over us. They feel thee not in the golden flood of the grapes, in the magic oil of the almond tree, and the brown juice of the poppy. They know not that it is thou who hauntest the bosom of the tender maiden, and makest a heaven of her lap; never suspect it is thou, the portress of heaven, that steppest to meet them out of ancient stories, bearing the key to the dwellings of the blessed, silent messenger of secrets infinite.
author: Novalis
work: Hymns to the Night, II, trans. George MacDonald
expansion: The second hymn opens by refusing the return of morning. Daylight is given a season; night's dominion is unbounded. What he calls unholy activity uses up the angel-visit of the night, the way labor uses up a dream. Sleep, he insists, is misunderstood by fools, who know only the shadow it casts in ordinary darkness. The real night is in the wine, the almond's oil, the poppy, in the beloved's body, and in the old stories whose teller arrives as heaven's portress, the silent messenger of infinite secrets. Night is a mode of knowledge and a mode of love. Day is the regime that keeps interrupting it.

Written after the death of Sophie von Kühn and revised for the Athenaeum, the hymn is Novalis's inversion of the Enlightenment identification of truth with light. The Aufklärung had made day the metaphor of maturity. Novalis, trained in the same philosophical century and steeped in Böhme, gives the sovereignty to night and treats daylight activity as a despotism. Böhme's dark ground, the Ungrund before the light of manifestation, is in the background: a depth that is prior to the world of distinct, busy things. The later hymns will turn this night toward Christ and a Christian eschatology. Hymn II is still the metaphysical inversion itself, before the narrative of redemption. MacDonald's Victorian English, slightly biblical, fits the poem's own scriptural cadence. Schiller and Goethe remain the daylight to which this is addressed. Novalis loved them and wrote from the other side of their sun.

The despotism of the earthly is a phrase for a life organized so that no visit can land. Unholy activity is the name, a century early, for a busyness that consumes the very experiences it is busy for. The hymn belongs with the appetite for silence, for sleep as something other than recovery-for-work, and for a knowledge that arrives in darkness, the apophatic register Novalis shares with the mystics without yet sounding like a monk. Night, in this poem, is the condition under which love's hidden sacrifice could burn without being spent. A culture that has made morning mandatory, and made every hour accountable, is the despot the hymn is asking to end.

The hymn's composition is part of the argument. Sophie von Kühn died in 1797. The Hymns to the Night were revised and published in the Athenaeum in 1800, inside the circle of the Schlegels, as a metaphysical poem and as a document of a life. Hymn II is still the inversion itself. The later hymns of the cycle turn the night toward Christ and toward an eschatological morning that would not be the despotism of the earthly. Reading II alone, as a permanent vote for darkness against day, flattens a sequence. The unbounded night is what has to be established before it can be given a Christian name.

Rilke, a century later, keeps a night and an angel and does not hand them to a church. The Duino Elegies inherit the Romantic wager that the dark is a mode of knowledge, and they spend it on the earth and on saying, which is a different expenditure from Novalis's. Böhme's Ungrund remains the speculative background of the hymn: a depth prior to the world of distinct, busy things. What the hymn adds, and what a culture of mandatory morning still has to hear, is the moral edge. Unholy activity consumes the visit. The night is a sovereignty that judges the day. It is not a technique of recovery in the service of tomorrow's labor.

quote: Amid heavenly odours he fell asleep, for Dream alone could lead him into the holy of holies. In marvellous mode Dream conducted him through endless rooms full of strange things, by means of witching sounds and changeful harmonies. All seemed to him so familiar, and yet strange with an unknown splendour; then vanished the last film of the perishable as if melted into air, and he stood before the celestial virgin. Then he lifted the thin glistening veil, and--Rosebud sank into his arms. A far-off music surrounded the mysteries of love's reunion and the outpouring of their longings, and shut out from the scene of their rapture everything alien to it.
author: Novalis
work: A parable from The Disciples at Saïs, trans. George MacDonald
expansion: Hyacinth has sought Isis across deserts and flowering countries, and at the sanctuary only dream is allowed to lead him in. Dream walks him through rooms of strange and familiar splendour, the last film of the perishable melts, and he stands before the celestial virgin. He lifts the thin veil. Rosebud, the girl he left, falls into his arms, and a distant music shuts the scene against everything alien to their reunion. The tale's whole journey, the old stranger, the unreadable book, the longing that would not let him stay, resolves in a recognition. The goddess and the beloved are one, and the organ that can bear that identity is dream.

The tale answers Schiller. In 'The Veil'd Image at Sais,' the youth who lifts the veil of Isis dies of what he sees; the prohibition is the point. Novalis, in The Disciples at Saïs, lets the lifting complete itself as a marriage. The sacred is the transfigured form of the near, and the way in is imaginal: dream, music, a space that is neither the ordinary room nor a concept. That structure is what Henry Corbin, reading Ibn Arabi, will later call the mundus imaginalis, a real world between sense and intellect, entered by a faculty of its own. Jung will read the same figure as anima, the inner beloved through whom the soul meets what it has projected outward as a goddess. Novalis is prior to both vocabularies. He has the scene. MacDonald translates it as a Märchen, and the lightness is part of the metaphysics. The holy of holies is reached in a story that still knows how to smile.

The relevance is the rehabilitation of dream and of love as organs of knowledge. A rationalism that allows dream only as discharge, and love only as preference, cannot read this ending at all. The music that closes the scene is the same intuition Schopenhauer will systematize and that the Romantics already trusted: a sound that draws a precinct around a revelation and keeps the alien out. For a mind drawn to the imaginal, to fairy tale as a serious form, and to the sense that the beloved is a figure of the soul's own depth, the lifted veil is the opposite of a disillusionment. What was sought at the end of the world was the face that had been nearest.

The tale is an answer with a date. Schiller's 'The Veiled Image at Sais' punishes the youth who lifts the veil. Novalis's Disciples at Saïs, written at the end of the 1790s and published in 1802, lets the lifting complete itself as a marriage, and only dream is allowed to conduct it. The mutation from prohibition to recognition is the Romantic decision about Isis: the sacred is the transfigured form of the near, and the organ that can bear the identity is imaginal. Henry Corbin's essay of 1964, naming the mundus imaginalis as a real world between sense and intellect, gives the ontological title to the room Hyacinth walks through. Jung's anima, and then James Hillman's, give it a psychological title.

Those later titles bring a danger Novalis does not yet face. Once the dream-room can be described as a content of the subject's psyche, Rosebud is no longer a figure one meets but a figure one has. Corbin spent his career refusing that reduction. The imaginal, for him, is a world, perceived by an organ, and not a department of the human interior. Novalis's lightness, the Märchen that still knows how to smile, is the form in which the recognition arrives before the quarrel between ontology and psychology has started. The quarrel is worth knowing, because it decides whether the lifted veil is a revelation or a projection.

quote: Nothing hinders the soul so much in attaining to the knowledge of God as time and place. Therefore, if the soul is to know God, it must know Him outside time and place, since God is neither in this or that, but One and above them. If the soul is to see God, it must look at nothing in time; for while the soul is occupied with time or place or any image of the kind, it cannot recognize God. If it is to know Him, it must have no fellowship with nothingness. Only he knows God who recognizes that all creatures are nothingness. For, if one creature be set over against another, it may appear to be beautiful and somewhat, but if it be set over against God, it is nothing. I say moreover: If the soul is to know God it must forget itself and lose itself, for as long as it contemplates self, it cannot contemplate God. When it has lost itself and everything in God, it finds itself again in God when it attains to the knowledge of Him, and it finds also everything which it had abandoned complete in God. If I am to know the highest good, and the everlasting Godhead, truly, I must know them as they are in themselves apart from creation. If I am to know real existence, I must know it as it is in itself, not as it is parceled out in creatures.
author: Meister Eckhart
work: Sermons, 'The Nearness of the Kingdom,' trans. Claud Field (1909)
expansion: The obstacle Eckhart names is precise. Time and place are what keep the soul from knowing God, because God is neither this nor that, but one, and above the pairs. While the soul is busy with a time, a place, or any image of that kind, it cannot recognize him. He then tightens the screw. To know God the soul must have no fellowship with nothingness, and the nothingness in question is the creature. Set beside another creature, a thing looks beautiful and like something. Set beside God, it is nothing. Knowing God therefore requires the soul to forget itself as well. Contemplating itself, it cannot contemplate him. Lost in God, it finds itself again, and finds everything it abandoned, now known in God rather than in the parceling-out of creation. Real existence is existence as it is in itself. Existence distributed among creatures is a knowing that has already missed it.

This is the vernacular via negativa, downstream of Dionysius and of the Neoplatonic One, preached in German to people who were not reading Proclus. Aquinas would say that creatures are nothing in the sense that they have no being of themselves, and he would guard the claim with analogy, so that creaturely being remains a real participation. Eckhart pushes the same scholastic point until the creature, confronted with God, is nothing without remainder, and until God is known by leaving images, including the image of oneself. The papal bull In agro dominico of 1329 will single out sentences of this family for condemnation. The danger the bull smelled is real: a nothingness of creatures can slide into a refusal of the created order, and a God beyond this and that can slide past the Incarnation. Field's 1909 English is an early and free rendering, often compressing the sermons. The argument in this passage is nonetheless the argument of Eckhart's German: God is not a being among beings, and the soul knows him by a loss.

The passage is a discipline for a life saturated with images, times, and self-observation. Every feed, every clock, every self-assessment is a this or a that, and the soul that lives among them is doing exactly what Eckhart says cannot recognize God. The recovery he describes, finding oneself and all things again inside the knowing of God, is the corrective to a purely negative reading. The nothingness is a passage, and the far side of it is a world known whole. That is the mystical form of the wish for a reality that is not parceled into contents. Heidegger's Gelassenheit, the releasement he explicitly learned from Eckhart, is the modern philosophical heir: a letting-be that stops grasping beings as inventory. The sermon is the older and sharper form.

The sentence about creaturely nothing has a scholastic guardrail and a speculative afterlife, and Eckhart walks between them in a way that satisfied neither. Aquinas holds that creatures are nothing of themselves and that their being is a real participation, secured by analogy, so that the goodness of creation is not a courtesy. The bull In agro dominico of 1329 isolates sentences of Eckhart's family for condemnation because the nothingness, pressed without remainder, can be heard as a refusal of the created order and as a God who has slipped past the Incarnation. Franz von Baader later brought the German sermons to Hegel's notice, and Hegel recognized a speculative mysticism near his own. That is a mutation from preaching to system. The sermon's demand that the soul forget itself becomes, in the logic, a moment in the self-movement of the concept. The loss is the loss of a practice.

Heidegger's 1955 memorial address turns the letting-go toward things in a technological world. Eckhart is named in the country-path conversation published with that address, where the word's older mystical use is the subject. Releasement is a stance in which beings are no longer seized as inventory. It is not the knowledge of God by the abandonment of creatures, which is what this sermon is for. Three nothings, then, and they should not be collapsed: Aquinas's participated nothing, Eckhart's nothing of the creature set over against God, Heidegger's refusal to grasp beings as stock. Field's 1909 English, free and early, is one of the doors through which the second of these reached readers before the critical edition. The argument in the passage is the argument of the German sermons even where Field compresses the wording.

quote: The highest act of renunciation for man is for God's sake to give up God, and that is what St Paul was willing to do; to give up all the blessings that he might receive from God. When for God's sake he gave up God, God still remained with him, since God's essence is Himself, not any impression or reception of Himself. He who does so is a true man to whom no grief may happen, any more than it happens to the Divine Being. There is a somewhat in the soul that is, as it were, a blood-relative of God. It is one, it has nothing in common with nothing, nor is it like nothingness, nothing. All that is created is nothing, all far from and foreign to the soul. Could I but find myself one instant in that sphere of pure existence, I should regard myself as little as a worm.
author: Meister Eckhart
work: Sermons, 'True Hearing' (Ecclesiasticus 24:30), trans. Claud Field (1909)
expansion: Field has Eckhart comment on Paul's wish to be cut off from God for the sake of his friends, and the comment goes to the limit of renunciation. The highest act is to give up God for God's sake: to let go of the blessings one might receive from God, and so of God as a good one holds. The paradox is immediate. In that giving up, God remained, because God's essence is himself and is never an impression or a reception of himself. The man who can do this is beyond grief in the way the divine being is beyond grief. Then the sermon names a somewhat in the soul, a blood-relative of God, one, with nothing in common with nothing, while everything created is nothing and foreign to the soul. One instant in that sphere of pure existence, Eckhart says, and he would think of himself as little as a worm.

The 'somewhat' is Field's English for the uncreated ground of the soul, the spark, the vünkelîn of the German sermons: something in the soul that is not a creature and so is not nothing. 'Blood-relative' is Field's homely metaphor, and it should be heard as a metaphor for kinship of being. The paradox of giving God up for God's sake is stated more nakedly in the sermon on poverty of spirit, where Eckhart prays to be made free of God. Field's 1909 version is a free early translation, and this paragraph has his cadences. The structure is Eckhart's own, and it is the structure Dionysius prepared when he set negation above affirmation: every conception of God, including the devout ones, is a conception, and the union lies past it. Paul's exile for love becomes, in Eckhart's hands, a metaphysical poverty. One releases God as an object so that what remains is God's own essence, which was never an object.

The passage is the cure for a religiosity, and equally for a secular longing, that is really an appetite for experiences of God, or of meaning, or of depth. Those are receptions. Eckhart's claim is that the highest act lets the receptions go, and that the letting-go is where the essence was all along. The spark, under whatever name, is his answer to the fear that this emptying is annihilation. There is something in the soul that the emptying does not touch, because it was never part of the created inventory. Contemporary spirituality often tries to collect states. The sermon is interested in the instant in which one would no longer bother to collect oneself. That instant is what the tradition calls detachment, and what Heidegger, reading Eckhart, tried to think as releasement. It is also the inner form of the Cloud's demand to mean God himself, and none of his goods.

The sharper statement of the paradox sits in the sermon on poverty of spirit, Beati pauperes spiritu, where Eckhart asks to be made free even of God. Field's 'True Hearing,' the sermon this extract comes from, is the same family in a milder cadence, and his phrase 'blood-relative of God' is his metaphor for the uncreated ground, the vünkelîn, not a sentence to cite from a critical text as if it were Eckhart's image. The structure under the metaphor is his: something in the soul is not a creature, and therefore is not the nothing that creatures are. Paul's willingness to be cut off for the sake of his brethren becomes, in this preaching, a metaphysical poverty. One releases God as a good one might receive, and what remains is God's essence, which was never a reception.

The modern recovery in English runs through renderings of this kind, Underhill and Inge among them, before Josef Quint's edition gave scholars a firmer German text. Thomas Merton's later reading of Eckhart takes the spark as a point of contact with Zen, a meeting Eckhart did not arrange and that belongs to the twentieth century's crossing of traditions. The use of the passage now is against a spirituality, religious or not, that collects states. Experiences of God, of meaning, of depth, are receptions. The highest act the sermon names lets the receptions go. The spark is the reason the letting-go is not annihilation. There is something the emptying does not touch, because it was never in the inventory.

quote: LIFT up thine heart unto God with a meek stirring of love; and mean Himself, and none of His goods. And thereto, look thee loath to think on aught but Himself. So that nought work in thy wit, nor in thy will, but only Himself. And do that in thee is to forget all the creatures that ever God made and the works of them; so that thy thought nor thy desire be not directed nor stretched to any of them, neither in general nor in special, but let them be, and take no heed to them. This is the work of the soul that most pleaseth God. All saints and angels have joy of this work, and hasten them to help it in all their might. All fiends be furious when thou thus dost, and try for to defeat it in all that they can. All men living in earth be wonderfully holpen of this work, thou wottest not how. Yea, the souls in purgatory be eased of their pain by virtue of this work. Thyself art cleansed and made virtuous by no work so much. And yet it is the lightest work of all, when a soul is helped with grace in sensible list, and soonest done. But else it is hard, and wonderful to thee for to do.
author: Anonymous
work: The Cloud of Unknowing, chapter 3, ed. Evelyn Underhill (1922)
expansion: The work of the book is stated as a direction of the heart. Lift it to God with a meek stirring of love, and mean God himself, none of his goods. Be unwilling to think on anything but him, so that nothing operates in wit or will except him. Forget every creature God ever made, and the works of those creatures, in general and in particular. Let them be. The author then stacks the consequences, and they are startling in their range. Saints and angels joy in this work and hurry to help it. Fiends are furious to defeat it. The living are helped by it in ways the worker does not know. The souls in purgatory are eased. The worker himself is cleansed by no work more. And the work is the lightest there is, when grace gives a felt desire, and the hardest when it does not.

This is the English Dionysian tradition in its practical form. The author writes in the late fourteenth century, in the line that runs from Dionysius through Thomas Gallus and the affective reading of the Mystical Theology: God is met above knowing, by a sharp love. 'None of his goods' is the same cut Eckhart makes between God and the gifts of God. Underhill's 1922 modernization, from the Harley manuscript, keeps the Middle English bone structure, including 'list' for felt longing. The chapter is a theory of hidden solidarity. A work done in private, with no content but a naked intent, is said to help the living and the dead. Contemplation is being described as a public act whose publicness is invisible. That claim separates this book from a merely psychological account of meditation, and from the devotional habit of thinking about holy things, which the author will later file under the cloud of forgetting.

The instruction is a counter-practice to a life of continuous reference: news, opinions, useful thoughts, even religious thoughts. Meaning God, and none of his goods, is a way of saying that the best things, once they become objects of mental possession, are already a distraction from the one thing. The lightness and the hardness belong together. When the desire is given, the work is nothing; when it is not, the work is almost impossible, and one does it anyway. That double description is still the best account of contemplative practice, and it is why the book remains the English classic for anyone who has given up on apologetics and still wants a work. The help it claims to give the world is not an argument. It is the claim that attention of this kind is already a form of charity.

The craft has a lineage of commentators before it has a lineage of modern readers. Thomas Gallus and the affective reading of Dionysius, more than the scholastic Dionysius of Albert and Aquinas, stand behind the instruction to mean God and none of his goods. Gallus had already set the summit of the Mystical Theology on the side of love. The Cloud turns an exegesis into a sequence of things to do, and it adds a claim Gallus's glosses do not make in this form: a private work of naked intent helps the living and the dead. Contemplation is described as a public act whose publicness cannot be seen. That is the chapter's own doctrine of the communion of saints, stated as a fact about attention.

Evelyn Underhill's edition of 1912, revised in 1922 from the manuscripts, is the book the modern recovery actually read. From it the chapter passes into the twentieth-century literature of contemplation, Merton's in particular, and into the secular literature of attention, Weil's and Murdoch's, which keep the cut between the one who is meant and the goods that are refused, and spend it on a neighbor or a kestrel rather than on God. The lightness and the hardness remain the best practical account. When a felt desire is given, the work is nothing. When it is not, the work is nearly impossible, and the instruction is to do it anyway. The help claimed for the world is the claim that this kind of attention is already a form of charity.

quote: But yet all reasonable creatures, angel and man, have in them each one by himself, one principal working power, the which is called a knowledgeable power, and another principal working power, the which is called a loving power. Of the which two powers, to the first, the which is a knowledgeable power, God that is the maker of them is evermore incomprehensible; and to the second, the which is the loving power, in each one diversely He is all comprehensible to the full. Insomuch that a loving soul alone in itself, by virtue of love should comprehend in itself Him that is sufficient to the full—and much more, without comparison—to fill all the souls and angels that ever may be. And this is the endless marvellous miracle of love; the working of which shall never take end, for ever shall He do it, and never shall He cease for to do it. See who by grace see may, for the feeling of this is endless bliss, and the contrary is endless pain.
author: Anonymous
work: The Cloud of Unknowing, chapter 4, ed. Evelyn Underhill (1922)
expansion: The author divides the principal working of every rational creature, angel or human, into two powers. The knowledgeable power finds God, its own maker, forever incomprehensible. The loving power finds him, in each creature differently, comprehensible to the full. A loving soul, by love alone, comprehends in itself the one who is enough to fill every soul and every angel that will ever be, and more, without comparison. He calls this the endless miracle of love. Its working will never finish, because God will never cease to do it. The feeling of it is endless bliss, and the absence of it endless pain. Knowledge is honored and then bounded. Love is given the office knowledge cannot hold.

The division is the affective Dionysianism of the thirteenth and fourteenth centuries, set against the scholastic ranking in which intellect is the higher power and beatitude is an act of seeing, with love as its consequence. Aquinas can say that in this life love sometimes reaches where knowledge does not, and still hold that the vision of God is intellectual. The Cloud author, for the work this book exists to teach, simply reverses the order of comprehension. God is incomprehensible to knowing and comprehensible to loving, and the comprehending is not a grasping of an object but a holding of the one who exceeds every vessel. The 'endless miracle' is that the finite soul, loving, contains the infinite, because the containing is God's own act and does not stop. Underhill's edition lets the scholastic vocabulary show through: knowledgeable power, loving power, principal working. This is a mystical theology with a faculty psychology, written so that a reader can locate the work in the will.

The chapter is a direct answer to the worry that unknowing is a blank. Unknowing is the condition of one power. The other power is in full comprehension, and the comprehension is bliss. For a reader who has come to distrust argument about God and has not therefore lost the wish to be related to God, the page draws the line exactly. Thought reaches a wall. Love is already on the other side of the wall, and what it holds is larger than all the knowers together. The contemporary relevance is the rehabilitation of love as a cognitive power, the thing Weil meant by attention and the thing the tradition meant by charity as a form of sight. A culture that trusts only the knowledgeable power will call this chapter poetry. The chapter's claim is that the knowledgeable power is the one that cannot finish the work.

The reversal has a precise scholastic counterpart. Aquinas holds that the beatitude of the life to come is an intellectual vision, and that love follows on sight, while allowing that in this life charity sometimes reaches where knowledge does not. The Cloud, for the single work it exists to teach, inverts the order of comprehension. God is incomprehensible to the knowledgeable power and comprehensible to the loving power, and the comprehending is God's own act, which does not stop. The finite soul holds the infinite because the holding is not the soul's achievement. Gallus prepared the inversion. This chapter states it as a faculty psychology a reader can locate in himself: two principal working powers, and only one of them can finish the work.

The secular mutation is Murdoch's, with Weil as the middle term. Attention, in The Sovereignty of Good, is a just and loving gaze at a reality other than oneself, and it is cognitive. It knows what the theories of the will, existentialist or behaviorist, do not know, because those theories have trusted only the knowledgeable power, the power that chooses or describes. The Cloud would not recognize a moral philosophy without God. The structure it would recognize is the one this chapter draws. Thought meets a wall. Love is already past the wall, and what it holds exceeds the vessels. A culture that calls this poetry has decided in advance that the knowledgeable power is the only one that counts as mind.

quote: AND if ever thou shalt come to this cloud and dwell and work therein as I bid thee, thee behoveth as this cloud of unknowing is above thee, betwixt thee and thy God, right so put a cloud of forgetting beneath thee; betwixt thee and all the creatures that ever be made. Thee thinketh, peradventure, that thou art full far from God because that this cloud of unknowing is betwixt thee and thy God: but surely, an it be well conceived, thou art well further from Him when thou hast no cloud of forgetting betwixt thee and all the creatures that ever be made. As oft as I say, all the creatures that ever be made, as oft I mean not only the creatures themselves, but also all the works and the conditions of the same creatures. I take out not one creature, whether they be bodily creatures or ghostly, nor yet any condition or work of any creature, whether they be good or evil: but shortly to say, all should be hid under the cloud of forgetting in this case.
author: Anonymous
work: The Cloud of Unknowing, chapter 5, ed. Evelyn Underhill (1922)
expansion: The cloud of unknowing is above, between the soul and God. The author now demands a second cloud, beneath, between the soul and every creature that has ever been made. The feeling of distance from God, he says, is a misreading. You are further from God when there is no cloud of forgetting between you and creatures than when the cloud of unknowing stands between you and God. 'Every creature' is then expanded until it cannot be dodged. It means the creatures and also their works and conditions, bodily and spiritual, good and evil. Nothing is exempted. All of it, in this work, goes under the cloud of forgetting. The good is included on purpose. A holy memory is still a memory, and in this work a memory is a between.

The chapter completes the architecture of the book. Unknowing without forgetting is sentiment, a lush feeling of God's distance accompanied by a mind full of objects. Forgetting without unknowing is amnesia. The two clouds are a single ascetic of attention, and the harder one, as he will insist, is the forgetting, because the creatures are near, interesting, and often genuinely good. Dionysius had said: leave behind sensible things and intelligible things. The English author translates that leave-taking into a practice of not looking. The shooter fixing his eye on the prick of the target, an image that follows just after this passage, makes the same point from the other side. What you behold, you stand under. To behold a creature, however excellent, is to put it above you and between you and God.

The inclusion of the good is the part that still offends. People will surrender distractions and cling to their best thoughts, their worthiest memories, their most refined self-images, and call the clinging spiritual life. The author files all of it in the same place. For a mind trying to pray, or simply to be quiet, in the middle of an endless archive of images, the cloud of forgetting is the only instruction that is actually usable. It is also the psychological insight the tradition had before psychology: attention is a placing of something above oneself. Choose what stands above you, because whatever you keep in mind is already occupying that height.

Dionysius says: leave behind sensible things and intelligible things. The English author turns the leave-taking into a rule about attention and memory. Whatever you keep in mind stands above you. A holy memory is still a between. The inclusion of the good is the chapter's severity, and it is the part that distinguishes this work from a general asceticism. He is not teaching contempt for creatures. He is teaching one work, in which every creature, good or evil, bodily or ghostly, goes under the cloud of forgetting so that the cloud of unknowing can be the only between. Ignatius of Loyola's counsel to find God in all things, two centuries later, is the complementary practice, and it is a different practice. Confusing them produces either a piety that cannot forget or a forgetting that has become a contempt.

The psychological insight is older than psychology. Attention is a placing. The archive of images a contemporary life carries, the best thoughts included, occupies the height the chapter reserves. The cloud of forgetting is usable in a way most mystical counsel is not, because it says what to do with the good, which is the thing people refuse to file. Unknowing without forgetting is a mood of distance with a full mind. Forgetting without unknowing is amnesia. The two clouds are one ascetic.

quote: For thou hast brought me with thy question into that same darkness, and into that same cloud of unknowing, that I would thou wert in thyself. For of all other creatures and their works, yea, and of the works of God's self, may a man through grace have fullhead of knowing, and well he can think of them: but of God Himself can no man think. And therefore I would leave all that thing that I can think, and choose to my love that thing that I cannot think. For why; He may well be loved, but not thought. By love may He be gotten and holden; but by thought never. And therefore, although it be good sometime to think of the kindness and the worthiness of God in special, and although it be a light and a part of contemplation: nevertheless yet in this work it shall be cast down and covered with a cloud of forgetting. And thou shalt step above it stalwartly, but listily, with a devout and a pleasing stirring of love, and try for to pierce that darkness above thee. And smite upon that thick cloud of unknowing with a sharp dart of longing love; and go not thence for thing that befalleth.
author: Anonymous
work: The Cloud of Unknowing, chapter 6, ed. Evelyn Underhill (1922)
expansion: The student asks how to think on God, and what God is. The author answers that the question has put him in the same cloud he wishes for the student. Creatures, their works, even the works of God, can be known and thought, by grace, to the full. God himself can be thought by no one. So the teacher would leave everything he can think, and choose for his love the thing he cannot think. The sentence that follows is the book's center: he may well be loved, and not thought; by love he may be gotten and held, and by thought never. Even the consideration of God's kindness, which is a light and a part of contemplation, is, in this particular work, to be put under the cloud of forgetting. One steps above it stalwartly and listily, with a devout stirring of love, and strikes the cloud with a sharp dart of longing, and does not leave for anything that happens.

'Listily,' set against 'stalwartly' by a 'but,' means deftly or skillfully. The step above holy thoughts is strong and also tactful. The longing is the devout stirring of love in the same sentence, and the sharp dart that follows. The chapter is the pastoral consequence of the two powers in chapter 4. Because God is incomprehensible to the knowledgeable power, the question 'what is he?' is a question the work cannot answer and should stop entertaining. Because he is comprehensible to love, the dart is the whole method. The author is careful about rank. Thinking of God's goodness is good, and is a part of contemplation. It is simply the wrong part for this work. That distinction saves the book from anti-intellectualism. Theology, meditation on the Passion, reflection on the divine attributes all have their place. They are the lights one agrees to step over when the work of unknowing begins. Underhill's text keeps the vernacular force of 'gotten and holden.' God is not concluded. He is held.

The dart of longing is the book's answer to the charge that negative theology is a refined emptiness. The cloud is thick, and one strikes it. The striking is love with an aim and without an image, and the instruction not to leave 'for thing that befalleth' is a rule of perseverance: consolations, desolations, and interruptions do not adjourn the work. For someone who has grown tired of religious argument and is still drawn to silence, this chapter is the operational core of the English mystical tradition. It is also a critique of the demand, now general, that everything worth loving be something one can think, define, and display. The highest object in the book is defined by the impossibility of that demand, and by the sufficiency of love.

The adverb is a textual argument, and the meaning is the other half of it. Underhill's 1922 text reads 'listily.' Sacred-texts, a reprint in wide circulation, reads 'Mistily,' which turns the word into blurred sight. That is a corruption, and the quotation rightly follows Underhill. 'Listily' means deftly or skillfully, the contrast with 'stalwartly.' The longing is already named in the stirring of love and in the dart. The method of the chapter depends on the dart. The dart is sharp. One strikes. The cloud is thick, and the instruction not to leave for anything that happens is a rule of perseverance through consolation and desolation alike. Thinking of God's kindness is granted to be good, and to be a part of contemplation, and to be the wrong part for this work. That ranking is what saves the book from a pose of anti-intellectualism.

John of the Cross, later and in another language, builds a systematic theology of the dark night that this chapter does not attempt. The Cloud is earlier, vernacular, and rude, and it is the English source rather than the Spanish one. Merton's contemplative books return to its center, that God is held by love and is not reached by thought, and they spend a life working out what the holding costs inside a monastery and then, later, outside one. The contemporary pressure the chapter still answers is the demand that whatever is worth loving be something one can define and display. The highest object in the book is specified by the failure of that demand, and by the sufficiency of a longing that has put its images down.

quote: Almost everyone declares that the symmetry of parts towards each other and towards a whole, with, besides, a certain charm of colour, constitutes the beauty recognised by the eye, that in visible things, as indeed in all else, universally, the beautiful thing is essentially symmetrical, patterned. But think what this means. Only a compound can be beautiful, never anything devoid of parts; and only a whole; the several parts will have beauty, not in themselves, but only as working together to give a comely total. Yet beauty in an aggregate demands beauty in details; it cannot be constructed out of ugliness; its law must run throughout. All the loveliness of colour and even the light of the sun, being devoid of parts and so not beautiful by symmetry, must be ruled out of the realm of beauty. And how comes gold to be a beautiful thing? And lightning by night, and the stars, why are these so fair? In sounds also the simple must be proscribed, though often in a whole noble composition each several tone is delicious in itself. Again since the one face, constant in symmetry, appears sometimes fair and sometimes not, can we doubt that beauty is something more than symmetry, that symmetry itself owes its beauty to a remoter principle?
author: Plotinus
work: Ennead I.6, On Beauty, trans. Stephen MacKenna (1917)
expansion: Plotinus states the opinion everyone holds and then dismantles it. Beauty, on that opinion, is symmetry of parts with each other and with the whole, plus a grace of color. He draws the consequence. Only a compound can be beautiful. A simple cannot. The parts of a beautiful whole are beautiful only as contributors, and yet a beautiful whole cannot be built out of ugly parts, so beauty has to run all the way down, which the definition cannot explain. Color and the light of the sun, having no parts, fall out of beauty altogether. So do gold, lightning, the stars. So does a single tone, loved in itself inside a composition whose beauty was supposed to be only the pattern. Last, a face keeps one symmetry and is sometimes fair and sometimes not. Symmetry owes its beauty to a remoter principle. The definition has failed on simples, on the same object at different moments, and, as the argument goes on to say, on virtue and on intellect, where there is nothing to measure.

The opinion he is wrecking is the Stoic and Hellenistic account of beauty as proportion, the account that will keep returning whenever beauty is reduced to a ratio. Plotinus's remoter principle is form, the presence of the intelligible in the sensible, which the rest of I.6 will describe as the soul recognizing its kin. This is why he, and not the theorists of proportion, becomes the source for a metaphysics of light: claritas in Aquinas's three marks of beauty, the sunlike eye in Goethe, the radiance that Romantic and symbolist aesthetics keep trying to name. Proportion is kept, and it is demoted to an instrument. A face can be evenly made and dead. A single color can be alive. MacKenna's 1917 English, from the first volume of his Enneads, has the slow forensic pace of the Greek. The passage is a cross-examination.

The cross-examination still works on every attempt to define beauty as balance, branding, or a measurable harmony of parts. Those accounts go silent in front of a patch of gold, a tone, a face whose proportions have not changed and whose beauty has. Plotinus's remoter principle is the opening through which beauty remains a metaphysical event. The passage shows that it is an arrival from elsewhere, and that the elsewhere is already implied by the things the symmetry theory has to rule out.

The definition he wrecks is the one that keeps returning whenever beauty is handed to a science of proportion. Stoic summetria, Vitruvius, the Renaissance canon of the body, the recurring faith in a golden section: each of them is the opinion the chapter states first and then breaks on simples. A patch of color, a single tone, gold, lightning, a face whose symmetry has not changed and whose beauty has, are the counter-examples. Aquinas receives the Platonic tradition with a triad, integrity, proportion, and claritas. Proportion is kept. Claritas, radiance, is the name of the remoter principle Plotinus is driving toward, the presence of form, which the rest of I.6 will describe as the soul recognizing its kin. Goethe's color and the sunlike eye live on that side of the triad, the side a ratio cannot capture.

Roger Scruton's defense of beauty, much later, as an address from a particular thing that asks to be contemplated for its own sake, is an aesthetic of claritas argued against both a subjectivism of preference and a functionalism of use. He does not need Plotinus's hypostases to inherit Plotinus's objection. If beauty were symmetry, it would be an engineering specification. The passage shows an arrival, and it shows that the things a symmetry theory has to rule out are already evidence for the arrival. That is the opening through which beauty remains a metaphysical event in this whole tradition, from the Enneads to the Romantic symbol and beyond it.

quote: And Nature, asked why it brings forth its works, might answer if it cared to listen and to speak:— "It would have been more becoming to put no question but to learn in silence just as I myself am silent and make no habit of talking. And what is your lesson? This; that whatsoever comes into being is my vision, seen in my silence, the vision that belongs to my character who, sprung from vision, am vision-loving and create vision by the vision-seeing faculty within me. The mathematicians from their vision draw their figures: but I draw nothing: I gaze and the figures of the material world take being as if they fell from my contemplation. As with my Mother (the All-Soul) and the Beings that begot me so it is with me: they are born of a Contemplation and my birth is from them, not by their Act but by their Being; they are the loftier Reason-Principles, they contemplate themselves and I am born."
author: Plotinus
work: Ennead III.8, On Nature, Contemplation, and the One, trans. Stephen MacKenna (1921)
expansion: Plotinus lets Nature speak, and the speech is a rebuke to the question. It would have been better to learn in silence, as Nature herself is silent and does not make a habit of talking. What comes into being is her vision, seen in that silence. She is sprung from vision, loves vision, and creates vision by the seeing power in her. Mathematicians look and then draw. She draws nothing. She gazes, and the figures of the material world take being as if they fell from the gaze. Her mother, the All-Soul, and the beings who begot her, gave her birth in the same way: by being, by contemplation, and not by an act added to their being. They contemplate themselves, and she is born. Production is the overflow of a seeing that does not deliberate.

The tractate's thesis, that everything is striving after contemplation, here reaches the bottom of the sensible world. Nature, which philosophers had treated as a blind maker or as a set of mechanisms, is a weak and silent intellect. The scale of seeing runs upward in clarity: nature, soul, intellect, where knower and known are one life. It does not culminate in the One. A pure unity, Plotinus says in this same tractate, has no room for vision and an object. The One is what the seeing is about. Bodies are what fall from nature's gaze. Making is a degraded contemplating, and contemplating is the original making. Schelling's philosophy of nature, in which productivity and the ideal are one act, is the nineteenth-century restatement. Goethe's demand that theory and beholding coincide, and his sense that nature is already at work as a kind of inwardness, belong to the same family, whether or not he is citing III.8. The speech is also a theology of silence. Nature's refusal to talk is the cosmological version of the mystic's refusal to conceptualize. The world is what a silence sees.

The passage turns the prestige of production upside down from the inside. Nature is the great producer, and she produces by not devising. A civilization that understands making only as planning, output, and design has forgotten the mode of making that Plotinus thought was the original one. The relevance for a love of the natural world is direct. A landscape is not a result. It is a gaze that has become visible, and the right answer to it, Nature says, is to learn in silence rather than to demand an account. Contemplation is restored as the high form of creativity, which is the point at which Plotinus, the Romantics, and the contemplative tradition are secretly one tradition.

Schelling's philosophy of nature is the nineteenth-century restatement, and the path of reading is indirect. Ficino's Latin Plotinus had already made the Enneads a philosophy of production rather than only a piety. Schelling's early books do not depend on Creuzer. The Ideas for a Philosophy of Nature is 1797 and the System of Transcendental Idealism is 1800; Creuzer's edition of Plotinus is 1835. In those two books, productivity and the ideal are one act seen from two sides. Nature is visible spirit. Goethe, suspicious of Schelling's system and allied with him against a merely mechanical nature, works the cousin claim on plants and on colors: beholding and theory are to coincide, and metamorphosis is a contemplation one can watch. Steiner, editing that Goethe and wanting a science of the spirit, turns Nature's speech into a discipline with exercises. The silence in which she says she creates becomes a curriculum of perception.

Barfield inherits Steiner's curriculum and Coleridge's imagination together, and the value of his work is the attempt to keep the insight without surrendering criticism. The speech in III.8 remains the original of the family. Making is a degraded and an overflowed contemplating. A civilization that understands production only as planning has forgotten the mode of making the tractate thinks is the first one. A landscape, on this account, is a gaze that has become visible. The instructed response is the one Nature gives the questioner: learn in silence. Contemplation is restored as the high form of creativity, which is where Plotinus, the Romantics, and the contemplative tradition are one tradition.

quote: In the same way, human beings, when weak on the side of contemplation, find in action their trace of vision and of reason: their spiritual feebleness unfits them for contemplation; they are left with a void, because they cannot adequately seize the vision; yet they long for it; they are hurried into action as their way to the vision which they cannot attain by intellection. They act from the desire of seeing their action, and of making it visible and sensible to others when the result shall prove fairly well equal to the plan. Everywhere, doing and making will be found to be either an attenuation or a complement of vision—attenuation if the doer was aiming only at the thing done; complement if he is to possess something nobler to gaze upon than the mere work produced.
author: Plotinus
work: Ennead III.8, On Nature, Contemplation, and the One, trans. Stephen MacKenna (1921)
expansion: The human case follows from Nature's. People who are weak on the side of contemplation still want vision, and they go looking for a trace of it in action. Unable to seize the vision inwardly, they are hurried into doing, so that the deed can be seen by themselves and shown to others, if it turns out reasonably like the plan. Doing and making, Plotinus concludes, are either an attenuation of vision or a complement of it. Attenuation, when the doer wanted only the thing done. Complement, when the doing exists so that there will be something nobler to look at than the work itself. Action is diagnosed as a desire to see, taking the long way because the short way is too hard.

Aristotle, in the last book of the Ethics, had already ranked the contemplative life above the political and practical lives, and called it the activity most like the gods'. He left moral action standing as a genuine human good for composite, embodied beings. Plotinus is harsher and more metaphysical. Action is what contemplation does when it fails to be itself. The complement clause saves him from mere contempt: a deed can be justified if it gives the soul a higher object of vision than the deed. The attenuation clause is the critique. Most busyness wants the product, and the product is a thinned vision. The passage is the ancient source of a suspicion the Romantics, Schopenhauer, and the contemplative writers share, that a life of projects is often a life that could not bear to look. Pieper's defense of leisure as the basis of culture is the twentieth-century restatement in Thomist language: the highest acts are useless in the way vision is useless.

Read now, the passage describes the economy of visibility. People act in order to see the action and to have it seen, and the plan is judged by whether the result can be shown. Plotinus would call that the trace left by a vision one was not strong enough to hold. The practical question he leaves is the complement: can the doing be ordered toward something nobler to gaze on than the work produced? Where it can, action is saved. Where it cannot, action is the shape weakness takes. For a reader tired of production as a moral identity, III.8 is the oldest and still the most exact account of why the tiredness is philosophical.

Aristotle, in the last book of the Ethics, ranks the contemplative life above the political and still defends the practical life as the good of a composite creature who is not a god. Plotinus is harsher. Action is what contemplation does when it cannot seize the vision, or it is a complement, justified when the deed gives the soul something nobler to look at than the deed. The contemplative tradition in the West, the Cloud and Eckhart among them, takes the harsh clause. Josef Pieper's Leisure the Basis of Culture, in 1948, is the Thomist mutation back toward Aristotle, stated against a society that has made total work the meaning of a life. Leisure is the condition of the acts that are useless in the way vision is useless.

Crawford's defense of skilled manual work is a further mutation, and it takes the complement clause as a program. A making in which the material pushes back can be a way of seeing, and the self is situated by the resistance. That is not Plotinus's preference. It is a modern attempt to find the contemplative dignity inside the work, so that action is saved from being only the trace of a vision one was too weak to hold. Read against the economy of visibility, in which people act in order to have the action seen, the passage is still the exact diagnosis. Where the doing is ordered toward something nobler to gaze on than the product, action is a complement. Where it is not, action is the shape the weakness takes.

quote: Every thing which is united is different from the one itself. For if it is united, it will participate in a certain respect of the one, so far as it is said to be united. That, however, which participates of the one, is both one and not one. But the one itself is not both one and not one. For if this were the case, again the one which is in it would have both these, and this would take place to infinity, there being no one itself at which it is possible to stop; but every thing being one and not one, there will be something united which is different from the one. For if the one is the same with the united, it will be infinite multitude. And in a similar manner each of the things of which the united consists will be infinite multitude.
author: Proclus
work: Elements of Theology, proposition IV, trans. Thomas Taylor (1816)
expansion: The proposition is small and the proof is a trap. Everything united is different from the One itself. To be united is to participate the One in some respect, and whatever participates the One is both one and not one. It is one by participation, and not one because participation implies a receiver that is other than the One. The One itself cannot be both one and not one. If it were, the one in it would again be both, and so on without a place to stop. There would be no One itself at which the regress ends. Therefore the united, the composite unity we actually meet, is different from the One. And if one identified them, the One would be an infinite multitude, since every united thing dissolves into further united things. The One is the principle that stops the dissolution. It is not itself a thing that has been unified.

This is henology, the science of the One, as distinct from ontology, the science of being. Plotinus had said that the One is beyond being. Proclus, in the Elements, turns that into a sequence of necessities a student can be examined on. Proposition IV is the moment the composite is forbidden to borrow the name of the principle. Taylor's 1816 English, printed with his translation of the Theology of Plato, is the version in which this logic reached English readers in the Romantic period; Blake's world knew Taylor's Plato, and Taylor's Proclus is the same labor. Dionysius depends on the distinction even where he does not cite it. When the Mystical Theology denies that God is any of the unities we can conceive, it is refusing to let the united stand in for the One. Eckhart's 'one, and above this and that' is the same refusal preached. Later scholarly English, above all Dodds's edition of 1933, is a better critical text. Taylor is the public, complete translation, and his propositions still carry the argument.

The proof is a piece of mental hygiene for anyone who uses the word unity. A unified life, a unified theory, a unified self, a unified culture: each of these is a participation, both one and not one, and none of them is the principle it participates. Confusing them with the One is how systems become idols. Proclus's regress is the formal version of the apophatic rule. Stop at a unity you have assembled, and you are still among composites; the series will ask for a further ground. The relevance to a perennialist instinct, and to the reading of Dionysius, is immediate. The One these writers are pointing at is precisely what cannot appear as a gathered whole. Every whole we can point to has already failed the test of proposition IV.

The proof enters Christian theology by a route that was demonstrated late. In 1895 Hugo Koch and Josef Stiglmayr showed, independently, that the author called Dionysius follows Proclus in detail. The henology of this proposition is therefore inside the Mystical Theology even where the Areopagite does not cite an Elements. Eriugena's Periphyseon carries the distinction of the One from every united thing into the Latin West. Aquinas, commenting on the Divine Names, labors to hold it together with analogy, so that the One beyond being is also the creator who gives the being of creatures. Eckhart's preaching of the One above this and that is less anxious about the guardrail. The united, the composite we can point to, is forbidden at every step to borrow the name of the principle.

Thomas Taylor's English of 1816, printed with his Plato, is the form in which Romantic London could meet the proof. Coleridge's Platonism and the milieu around Blake knew Taylor's labors, whatever particular page they had open. E. R. Dodds's edition of 1933 is a different event: a critical text for classicists, no longer a Romantic scripture, and a better guide to the Greek. Taylor remains the public, complete translation in which the argument did its historical work. The hygiene the proof offers is unchanged. A unified self, a unified theory, a unified culture, is a participation, both one and not one. Treating it as the One is how a composite becomes an idol. The regress is the formal version of the apophatic rule.

quote: For if multitude is prior to the one, the one indeed will participate of multitude, but multitude which is prior to the one will not participate of the one, since that multitude existed prior to the subsistence of the one. For it will not participate of that which is not; because that which participates of the one, is one and at the same time not one; but the one will not yet subsist, that which is first being multitude. It is, however, impossible that there should be a certain multitude, which in no respect whatever participates of the one. Multitude, therefore, is not prior to the one.
author: Proclus
work: Elements of Theology, proposition V, trans. Thomas Taylor (1816)
expansion: Proposition V is the companion proof, run as a reductio. Suppose multitude were prior to the One. Then the One would participate multitude, while multitude, being prior, would not participate the One, since the One would not yet be there to participate. Participation in what is not is nothing. And a multitude that in no respect participates the One is impossible: each of its members would be a multitude, and each of those another, an infinite of infinites, with nothing one anywhere for the division to stop. Therefore multitude is not prior to the One. The One is first because, without a prior unity, many cannot even be many. Manyness is a late condition. It presupposes the principle it seems to threaten.

Together with proposition IV, this is the opening move of the whole Proclean system. Procession, the derivation of lower orders from higher, can begin only once the One is safe from two confusions: from being a composite, and from being secondary to the many. Christian Platonism inherits both safeguards. Dionysius's God is the cause of all multitude and is not a member of it. Creation, in the scholastic development, will restate the priority as the priority of simple being over composed beings, with differences Proclus would not accept, since he does not have a creator in the biblical sense. The logical nerve travels anyway. Taylor's translation makes the nerve available in the English in which Coleridge, and the Platonic undercurrent of Romanticism, could meet it. The proof is also why 'the many' is never, in this tradition, a first principle. Atomism, pluralism, and the prestige of sheer variety are, by this argument, descriptions of something that has already fallen from a unity they depend on.

The reductio is a good instrument against the assumption, now nearly invisible, that plurality is the natural starting point and unity a late, optional achievement, something groups and theories may or may not reach. Proclus says the many cannot be there first. A world of items, data, and positions still owes its countability to a one it does not contain. That is a metaphysical claim, and it is also a contemplative one: attention that stops at the scatter has stopped too soon, because the scatter was never able to found itself. The passage is the driest page in this set, and it is the floor under the others. Eckhart's One above this and that, Dionysius's God beyond every name, Plotinus's source of beauty, all of them require that the principle be prior to the multitude of things it makes beautiful, knowable, and real.

Christian Platonism inherits the priority and changes the verb. Proclus's One does not choose, and it does not make a world from nothing. Creation, as the scholastics develop it, restates the dependence of the many on the One as the free gift of being by a God who is not a member of the series. That is a mutation the Elements will not underwrite, and the logical nerve travels anyway: multitude cannot be there first. Dionysius's God is the cause of all multitude and is not an item in it. The perennialist reading, Guénon's in particular, takes the same priority as evidence that the great traditions agree on a first principle. The agreement, such as it is, begins only after this proof. Everything that distinguishes emanation from creation, and a metaphysical One from the God of Abraham, is a later decision about how the dependence is told. Flattening those decisions is not what proposition V says.

The contemporary assumption the reductio still cuts against is quiet and nearly invisible. Plurality is treated as the natural starting point, and unity as an optional late achievement of groups and of theories. Proclus says the many cannot found themselves. A world of items, data, and positions owes its countability to a one it does not contain. The contemplative form of that claim is the one the rest of this set keeps spending: attention that stops at the scatter has stopped too soon. Eckhart's One above this and that, Dionysius's God beyond every name, and Plotinus's source of beauty all require the principle to be prior to the multitude of things it makes real.

quote: Concrete ideas are formed by us on the basis of our concepts by means of the imagination. Hence what the free spirit needs in order to realise his concepts, in order to assert himself in the world, is moral imagination. This is the source of the free spirit’s action. Only those men, therefore, who are endowed with moral imagination are, properly speaking, morally productive. Those who merely preach morality, i.e., those who merely excogitate moral rules without being able to condense them into concrete ideas, are morally unproductive. They are like those critics who can explain very competently how a work of art ought to be made, but who are themselves incapable of the smallest artistic production.
author: Rudolf Steiner
work: The Philosophy of Spiritual Activity, trans. R. F. Alfred Hoernlé (1922 edition)
expansion: Moral imagination is Steiner's name for the act that makes a free agent. A concept of what ought to be done stays inert until imagination condenses it into a concrete idea, fitted to a perceptible situation. The people he calls morally unproductive are the ones who can say how an action ought to look and cannot produce one. He reaches for the analogy of the critic who knows how a work of art should be made and cannot make the smallest one. Freedom, in this book, is the capacity to determine from oneself the ideas that will underlie action. A mechanical process does not do it, and a God standing outside the agent does not do it either.

The book is the early Steiner, the Philosophy of Freedom of 1894, in the Hoernlé English of 1916 as revised for the 1922 edition. It is a philosophy of ethical individualism written before anthroposophy became a movement with exercises and a cosmology. He is arguing with Kant. The categorical imperative, a law that arrives as a command from beyond the agent's own insight, is exactly what moral imagination is there to replace. He is also arguing with a crude evolutionary ethics that would measure a new moral idea by an old species and call the new one degenerate. A new moral idea is no more illegitimate, on his monism, than a new organic form.

Goethe is the method behind the argument even where this chapter is talking about conduct. Steiner had edited Goethe's scientific writings and taken metamorphosis as the pattern of a thinking that stays with the phenomenon and lets a form transform. Moral imagination is metamorphosis in the practical sphere: a principle becomes an individual deed without being copied from a template. Barfield will later treat this, together with Coleridge, as the seed of a conscious participation. The danger, which Steiner himself notes against immature readers, is that an undeveloped impulse announces itself as a moral intuition. The theory is about a mature spirit's concrete idea, and it is an account of freedom as productivity.

quote: It is not the task of knowledge to reproduce in conceptual form something already existing independently. Its task is to create a wholly new realm which, united with the world of sense-data, ends by yielding us reality in the full sense. In this way, man’s supreme activity, the creative productivity of his spirit, finds its organic place in the universal world-process. Without this activity it would be impossible to conceive the world-process as a totality complete in itself. Man does not confront the world-process as a passive spectator who merely copies in his mind the events which occur, without his participation, in the cosmos without. He is an active co-creator in the world-process, and his knowledge is the most perfect member of the organism of the universe. This view carries with it an important consequence for our conduct, for our moral ideals. These, too, must be regarded, not as copies of an external standard, but as rooted within us. Similarly, we refuse to look upon our moral laws as the behests of any power outside us. We know no “categorical imperative” which, like a voice from the Beyond, prescribes to us what to do or to leave undone.
author: Rudolf Steiner
work: The Philosophy of Spiritual Activity, appendix on Truth and Science, trans. R. F. Alfred Hoernlé (1922 edition)
expansion: The appendix states the epistemology the ethics depends on. Knowing is not the copying of a world that is already finished without the knower. Thinking produces a content of its own, and only when that content is united with what the senses give is there reality in the full sense. The human being is therefore a co-creator in the world-process, and knowledge is, in his phrase, the most perfect member of the organism of the universe. Hoernlé's English says the events occur 'in the cosmos without,' meaning the cosmos outside the spectator. The stiffness is the translator's. The claim is that the spectator-picture of knowledge is already a false moral picture, because it makes the agent someone who receives ends from elsewhere.

From the epistemology he draws the consequence for ideals. They are rooted in the agent. There is no voice from the Beyond prescribing what to do or to leave undone. He names Kant's categorical imperative in order to refuse it. Moral ideals are free creations. This is the same refusal the chapter on moral imagination makes from the side of action, here made from the side of truth. A truth that is only a copy cannot found a freedom. A truth that is an act can.

The mutation into later Steiner, and then into Barfield, is the mutation of a critical point into a story about consciousness. Here the co-creation is the ordinary, if usually unnoticed, work of thinking joining percepts. In the anthroposophical writings the same conviction becomes a path of higher knowledge, with definite exercises. Barfield's final participation is the historical form: a culture that has withdrawn from participation in its representations could come to participate again, knowingly, without returning to an archaic fusion. Goethe's irony, the demand to theorise while knowing that one is theorising, is the safeguard this appendix does not yet emphasize. Co-creation without that irony becomes the fantasy that the spirit posits the world. Held with the irony, it is the claim that a world described as if no one were thinking it has not been fully described.

quote: Duration is the continuous progress of the past which gnaws into the future and which swells as it advances. And as the past grows without ceasing, so also there is no limit to its preservation. Memory, as we have tried to prove, is not a faculty of putting away recollections in a drawer, or of inscribing them in a register. There is no register, no drawer; there is not even, properly speaking, a faculty, for a faculty works intermittently, when it will or when it can, whilst the piling up of the past upon the past goes on without relaxation. In reality, the past is preserved by itself, automatically. In its entirety, probably, it follows us at every instant; all that we have felt, thought and willed from our earliest infancy is there, leaning over the present which is about to join it, pressing against the portals of consciousness that would fain leave it outside.
author: Henri Bergson
work: Creative Evolution, chapter 1, trans. Arthur Mitchell (1911)
expansion: Duration, in the opening of Creative Evolution, is the past gnawing into the future and swelling as it advances. Memory is not a faculty that files recollections in a drawer. The past preserves itself. In its entirety it leans on the present, and the brain's work, as he will say in the next sentences, is mostly to hold it back so that action can go forward. What matters in the sentences here is the refusal of a psychology of states. If inner life were solid beads on a solid thread, there would be no duration. The beads are what attention and language make when they need something logic can handle. Under the symbols, time is the stuff of psychical life.

The book of 1907 applies to life a result he had argued in 1889, in Time and Free Will: real duration is undivided continuity and creation, and it is falsified as soon as it is spread out in space. Mitchell's 1911 English is the translation in which the book reached many American and British readers. William James, who died in 1910, had been the sympathetic reader of the French Creative Evolution of 1907, not of this translation. The mutation from the early essay to Creative Evolution is the mutation from a psychology of consciousness to a metaphysics of the living world. The past that presses on the present becomes the pattern of an élan, a vital impetus, which he will oppose both to a mechanism in which everything is given and to a finalism in which the end is given.

The page still cuts against a picture of the self as a sequence of replaceable states, a profile, a dataset, a present with no weight. Character, he says in the sentences that follow these, is the condensation of a history, and we desire with the whole of it even when we think with a small part. That is why a moment cannot be repeated. The circumstances might return. The person they would meet has already been changed by having lived them. Irreversibility is the moral fact inside the metaphysics. A culture of resets and of optimized presents is a culture that has chosen the drawer.
