quote: This is what the cinematograph does. With photographs, each of which represents the regiment in a fixed attitude, it reconstitutes the mobility of the regiment marching. It is true that if we had to do with photographs alone, however much we might look at them, we should never see them animated: with immobility set beside immobility, even endlessly, we could never make movement. In order that the pictures may be animated, there must be movement somewhere. The movement does indeed exist here; it is in the apparatus. It is because the film of the cinematograph unrolls, bringing in turn the different photographs of the scene to continue each other, that each actor of the scene recovers his mobility; he strings all his successive attitudes on the invisible movement of the film. The process then consists in extracting from all the movements peculiar to all the figures an impersonal movement abstract and simple, movement in general, so to speak: we put this into the apparatus, and we reconstitute the individuality of each particular movement by combining this nameless movement with the personal attitudes. Such is the contrivance of the cinematograph. And such is also that of our knowledge. Instead of attaching ourselves to the inner becoming of things, we place ourselves outside them in order to recompose their becoming artificially.
author: Henri Bergson
work: Creative Evolution, chapter 4, trans. Arthur Mitchell (1911)
expansion: The cinematograph is his model of the intellect at work on becoming. Snapshots of a marching regiment, each one a fixed attitude, are thrown in rapid succession, and the mobility seems to return. It returns only because there is movement in the apparatus, the unrolling of the film. From the particular movements one has extracted an impersonal movement-in-general, put it in the machine, and recombined it with the attitudes. Knowledge, he says, does the same. It places itself outside the inner becoming of things and recomposes that becoming artificially. Perception, intellection, and language are this contrivance. Ordinary knowledge is cinematographical.

The polemic is aimed at a way of thinking he traces from Zeno's paradoxes to the Platonic idea and on into modern science. The idea, eidos, is a stable view taken of an instability, a snapshot that has had its thread to time cut and has then been treated as more real than the change. He is not dismissing Plato's whole ambition. He is saying that a metaphysics built by the cinematographical habit will always set eternity above time, and will always be surprised that the snapshots, set beside one another, never quite yield the movement. The practical success of the habit is not in dispute. Action needs stops. Speculation that uses only stops misses what life is doing.

Proust, who was related to Bergson by marriage and who built a novel on involuntary memory, is the literary mutation: the past returns as a whole, not as a fact retrieved from storage, which is what the first chapter's account of duration had described. Deleuze's Bergsonism, much later, makes the virtual and the actual into a philosophy of cinema itself, a reversal in which the apparatus Bergson used as a figure of illusion becomes an art that can think time. The figure's original force is the simpler one. A sequence of states is not a life. The movement is in the apparatus, or it is nowhere. Attention that wants the real has to get inside the transition the snapshots were taken to avoid.

quote: Yet if the only form of tradition, of handing down, consisted in following the ways of the immediate generation before us in a blind or timid adherence to its successes, “tradition” should positively be discouraged. We have seen many such simple currents soon lost in the sand; and novelty is better than repetition. Tradition is a matter of much wider significance. It cannot be inherited, and if you want it you must obtain it by great labour. It involves, in the first place, the historical sense, which we may call nearly indispensable to anyone who would continue to be a poet beyond his twenty-fifth year; and the historical sense involves a perception, not only of the pastness of the past, but of its presence; the historical sense compels a man to write not merely with his own generation in his bones, but with a feeling that the whole of the literature of Europe from Homer and within it the whole of the literature of his own country has a simultaneous existence and composes a simultaneous order. This historical sense, which is a sense of the timeless as well as of the temporal and of the timeless and of the temporal together, is what makes a writer traditional. And it is at the same time what makes a writer most acutely conscious of his place in time, of his contemporaneity.
author: T. S. Eliot
work: The Sacred Wood, 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' (1920)
expansion: Tradition, in the essay of 1919 collected the next year, is a labor, not an inheritance. Following the previous generation is the form of it he thinks should be discouraged. Novelty is better than that kind of repetition. What he requires instead is the historical sense: the pastness of the past and the presence of the past, felt together, so that the literature of Europe from Homer, and the literature of one's own country inside it, exists simultaneously and composes an order. That sense is what makes a writer traditional, and it is what makes him know his own contemporaneity. The timeless and the temporal are not alternatives. The sense of them together is the qualification.

The essay belongs to the early Eliot, the critic of The Sacred Wood, before the conversion of 1927 and before Four Quartets. Its immediate enemies are a Romantic cult of the poet's difference and a Georgian comfort with the previous generation's successes. The individuality worth having, he has just argued, is often the place where the dead poets assert themselves most vigorously. The historical sense is the condition for that individuality. It is also the seed of the later poems' concern with time. What the essay states as a principle of criticism, the poems will try to live as a pattern of moments in which a life is answerable to more than its succession.

The responsibility he names is easy to sentimentalize into a respect for the canon. Read strictly, it is harder. The existing order is complete before the new work arrives, and for order to persist the whole order has to be, however slightly, altered. The past is changed by the present. Conformity of the kind that leaves both untouched is not conformity. A writer who wants the tradition as a shelter from the present has missed the essay. A writer who wants the present as a liberation from the dead has missed it too. The labor is the labor of holding both, which is the labor Four Quartets will not let him set down.

quote: Blake was endowed with a capacity for considerable understanding of human nature, with a remarkable and original sense of language and the music of language, and a gift of hallucinated vision. Had these been controlled by a respect for impersonal reason, for common sense, for the objectivity of science, it would have been better for him. What his genius required, and what it sadly lacked, was a framework of accepted and traditional ideas which would have prevented him from indulging in a philosophy of his own, and concentrated his attention upon the problems of the poet. Confusion of thought, emotion, and vision is what we find in such a work as _Also Sprach Zarathustra_; it is eminently not a Latin virtue. The concentration resulting from a framework of mythology and theology and philosophy is one of the reasons why Dante is a classic, and Blake only a poet of genius. The fault is perhaps not with Blake himself, but with the environment which failed to provide what such a poet needed; perhaps the circumstances compelled him to fabricate, perhaps the poet required the philosopher and mythologist; although the conscious Blake may have been quite unconscious of the motives.
author: T. S. Eliot
work: The Sacred Wood, 'Blake' (1920)
expansion: The essay praises Blake's eye and then refuses his system. A remarkable sense of language, a gift of hallucinated vision, and a real understanding of human nature were, Eliot thinks, left without the framework that would have concentrated them. Impersonal reason, common sense, the objectivity of science, a mythology and a theology already accepted: these would have kept Blake on the problems of the poet. Instead, Eliot says, England handed him an empty place where a continuous religious history might have been, and he fabricated a philosophy out of odds and ends, ingenious in the way homemade furniture is ingenious. Dante is a classic because of the concentration a traditional framework gives. Blake remains a poet of genius. The fault is charged as much to the environment as to the man.

The judgment is 1920, and it is a young classicist's judgment. It sits beside 'Tradition and the Individual Talent' as the case study. Blake is what a great gift does when the historical sense has no order to join. Eliot's example of the confusion of thought, emotion, and vision is Nietzsche's Zarathustra, which tells you which kind of homemade metaphysics he is unwilling to admire. The Latinity he wants is Dante's, a philosophy inside the poem because it was the philosophy of a world, not a philosophy the poet had to invent in order to have a world.

Kathleen Raine's life's work is the argued reply. In Blake and Tradition and in Defending Ancient Springs she holds that Blake's mythology is learned, a reception of Plato, Plotinus, Boehme, and the Hermetic writings, and that what Eliot called odds and ends is a tradition he had not recognized. The mutation is a lesson in how a criticism creates the scholarship that overturns it. Eliot's demand for a framework remains serious. Raine's claim is that Blake had one, and that the English suspicion of visionary poetry as crankiness is a failure to read the framework. Between them is the question this whole set keeps meeting: whether imagination is a private fabrication or an organ that joins a real order.

quote: The essence of original participation is that there stands behind the phenomena, and on the other side of them from me, a represented which is of the same nature as me.
author: Owen Barfield
work: Saving the Appearances: A Study in Idolatry (New York: Harcourt, Brace & World, 1965), p. 42
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. Barfield treats the history of language as a history of the splitting of meanings. In early speech, what we now separate as the literal and the metaphorical was one concrete figure. The word did not point at a bare object and then, optionally, decorate it. Object and meaning arrived together. Poetic Diction argues that poetry is the place where that lost unity can be remembered and, in flashes, restored. Saving the Appearances extends the claim from words to perception. Original participation is his name for a consciousness in which the world is experienced as meaningful from within, not as a set of objects represented to a subject standing outside them. The scientific revolution, as he reads Galileo, Locke, and the new experimental philosophy, withdraws that participation. What remains are collective representations, appearances produced by a culture, which the culture then takes for things in themselves. He calls that mistake idolatry. Final participation would be a free, conscious recovery of participation, chosen rather than inherited, and it would not be a return to the archaic fusion.

The reading list behind the claim is specific. Coleridge's distinction of imagination from fancy, and his struggle with a dead world of objects, is the Romantic source. Goethe's way of science, in which the observer and the phenomenon belong to one act, is the second. Steiner's Philosophy of Freedom and the later anthroposophy are the third, and Barfield defended them in public, including in Romanticism Comes of Age, while trying to keep a critical standard Steiner's movement did not always want. The Inklings argued the consequence. Lewis conducted a long correspondence with Barfield, their Great War, resisting what he heard as a slide into subjectivism. Tolkien's sense that language is not a code laid over a finished world carries the mark of Barfield's theory of meaning.

Set beside this set of passages, Barfield is the historian of a change the others describe from inside. Goethe's sunlike eye and his irony about theorising are, in Barfield's terms, exercises of participation that know themselves as exercises. Plotinus's soul recognizing its kin in the beautiful is an ancient form of the same kinship. Charles Taylor will later describe the buffered self and the immanent frame as the felt result of the withdrawal, without Barfield's prescription of a final participation. Jean Gebser's structures of consciousness are a cousin map, drawn independently. The likeness is real. A line of reading from Gebser to Barfield should not be invented.

The present use is a diagnosis of representation. A life conducted on screens, models, and metrics is a life inside idolatry in his exact sense: appearances taken for the things. The remedy he hoped for was not less thinking. It was a thinking that participates again, knowingly. That hope is the modern form of Goethe's demand to theorise with irony, and of Steiner's claim that knowledge is a co-creation. It is also the reason his work belongs with a love of landscape and of poetic speech. Both are, for him, evidence that meaning is not a coating we add to a bare world.

quote: In its fairy-tale — or otherworld — setting, it is a sudden and miraculous grace: never to be counted on to recur.
author: J. R. R. Tolkien
work: “On Fairy-Stories,” in The Tolkien Reader (New York: Del Rey / Random House, 1966), p. 86
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. The lecture, given as the Andrew Lang lecture in 1939 and published in 1947 in a volume in honor of Charles Williams, defends the fairy-story as a serious form and refuses the idea that it is native to children. Tolkien distinguishes three faces of the art he calls recovery, escape, and consolation. Recovery is a regaining of sight, so that things long dulled by familiarity are seen again as what they are. Escape he defends as the escape of a prisoner, and he refuses the sneer that calls it desertion. Consolation is the sudden joyous turn he names eucatastrophe, the opposite of the tragic catastrophe, a grace of the story's ending that does not deny the sorrow it answers. Around these he sets sub-creation: the making of a secondary world with the inner consistency of reality. The human maker works with what is already given, and the making is a real making. He then makes the theological wager that the Christian story has the shape of a fairy-story that has entered history, so that the joy the art offers is answered by a truth of the same shape.

The lecture is an Inkling argument, addressed to the same room as Williams's doctrine of exchange and Lewis's long defense of myth as a vehicle of truth. Tolkien had reservations about George MacDonald, whose fairy tales he found mixed, and he had none about the dignity of the form. Coleridge's imagination is in the background of sub-creation. Barfield's account of meaning is in the background of the claim that the fantastic is a way of seeing and not a coating on the real. The publication in a book for Williams matters. Eucatastrophe and coinherence are neighboring answers to the question of how a sorrow and a joy can inhabit one story without either cancelling the other.

The mutation from Romantic wonder to this lecture is the addition of history. Novalis can lift the veil inside a dream and find the beloved. Tolkien wants a turn that is still a turn of story and that he is willing to say has happened in the primary world. That is his difference from a symbolism that never risks a fact, and from a realism that never risks a joy. Lewis, moving in the same years from a love of myth toward a claim about fact, is the parallel case, argued in a different temperament.

The lecture is a criticism of a culture that files wonder under childhood and files adulthood under disenchantment. Recovery is a discipline of attention: the trite thing, seen again, is the test. Escape, in his sense, judges a world by whether a reasonable person would want to flee it, and it calls the wish sanity. Consolation refuses the prestige of the unhappy ending. For a reader drawn to myth, to the imaginal, and to a Christianity that does not apologize for joy, the essay is the twentieth-century statement of why those loves are one love.

Tolkien distinguishes three faces of the art he calls recovery, escape, and consolation. Recovery is a regaining of sight, so that things long dulled by familiarity are seen again as what they are. Escape he defends as the escape of a prisoner, and he refuses the sneer that calls it desertion. Consolation is the sudden joyous turn he names eucatastrophe, the opposite of the tragic catastrophe, a grace of the story's ending that does not deny the sorrow it answers. Around these he sets sub-creation: the making of a secondary world with the inner consistency of reality. The human maker works with what is already given, and the making is a real making. He then makes the theological wager that the Christian story has the shape of a fairy-story that has entered history, so that the joy the art offers is answered by a truth of the same shape.

quote: We are supposed to be content to “cast our burdens on the Lord.” The Lord indicated that the best way to do so was to hand these over to someone else to cast, or even to cast them on him in someone else.
author: Charles Williams
work: He Came Down from Heaven (London: Faber and Faber, 1950), p. 88
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. Williams's distinctive doctrine is coinherence. No being exists enclosed in itself. Lives inhere in one another, and the City of God is the social form of that fact, practiced under the conditions of the fall as exchange and substitution: one person can bear what is properly another's, and the bearing is a real spiritual act, not a metaphor for sympathy. He founded a small order, the Companions of the Co-inherence, whose members undertook substitutions of this kind. Beside the doctrine he sets two ways, both necessary. The way of the affirmation of images takes the body, romantic love, the city, and the beloved as doors. Dante's Beatrice is his great case, and The Figure of Beatrice is the book of it. The way of the rejection of images is the negative way, the stripping that the Cloud and John of the Cross practice. Each way corrects the other. Affirmation without rejection becomes idolatry of the image. Rejection without affirmation becomes a hatred of the creation through which glory actually arrives.

The sources are Dante, the theology of the Body of Christ as a real coinherence of members, and a novelist’s sense of the city of London as already a web of substituted lives. Eliot published him at Faber and wrote on him after his death in 1945. Lewis’s Arthurian poetry and The Four Loves are marked by the doctrine of exchange. Auden read him with an admiration that left traces in the later poems. Williams is the Inkling whose theology is least easily reduced to apologetics, because the claim is metaphysical and practical at once: the way things are is that we are in one another, and the way to live is to bear one another on purpose.

Set against the negative tradition in this set, he is the advocate of the other half. The Cloud’s cloud of forgetting is the rejection of images, and Williams would say it is true and incomplete. Eckhart’s letting-go of God for God’s sake is the extreme of rejection. Beatrice is the extreme of affirmation, a creature through whom glory is seen without the creature being dissolved into a mere sign. The Romantic marriage of Hyacinth and Rosebud is a tale of affirmation. Williams gives that tale a dogmatic name and a practice.

The relevance is the repair of a split the modern reader of mysticism often chooses instead of suffering. One camp keeps the images and loses the God. The other keeps the unknowing and loses the world. Williams’s claim is that the two ways are one life, and that substitution is how the life becomes social. A culture of buffered selves, each the proprietor of a private interior, is the practical denial of coinherence. His books are the twentieth-century English argument that the denial is false to the way persons actually exist.

quote: Every one of us is shadowed by an illusory person: a false self. This is the man I want myself to be but who cannot exist, because God does not know anything about him. And to be unknown of God is altogether too much privacy.
author: Thomas Merton
work: New Seeds of Contemplation (New York: New Directions, 1972), p. 34
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. Merton distinguishes a false self from a true one. The false self is the social ego, built of desires, fears, and the roles a life uses to make itself feel real. The true self is hidden in God and is not identical with those roles. Contemplation, as New Seeds of Contemplation describes it, is not a psychological state one produces by technique. It is a gift of unknowing, a simple intuition born of love, closer to the Cloud of Unknowing and to John of the Cross than to a method of mental silence. The early Merton, in The Seven Storey Mountain and the first Seeds of Contemplation, can sound like a flight from the world. The later journals, Conjectures of a Guilty Bystander and the Asian Journal, revise that flight. Contemplation is worked out inside history, in friendship with the world, and in a serious meeting with Zen. The false self remains the problem. The world is no longer the name of it.

He read the English mystics in Underhill’s recovery of them, and he read Eckhart seriously in the 1950s and 1960s, taking the spark, the uncreated ground, as the point where a Christian account of the self and a Zen account of emptiness could speak. That meeting is his own mutation of Eckhart, who did not know Zen. Weil’s attention is a parallel modern discipline, more moral and less monastic. Merton’s version stays inside a vowed life even when the later books open the monastery gates. The lineage behind the false self runs from the Pauline old man through the Desert Fathers’ logismoi, the distracting thoughts, to the Cloud’s warning that a person may love the goods of God in place of God.

The change from the early books to the late ones is the change to watch. A contemplation defined against the world becomes a contemplation that can love the world without confusing the world with the self. That is the twentieth-century form of Williams’s two ways, lived by a monk who began on the way of rejection and had to learn affirmation without abandoning the cell. His journals are the record of the learning.

The false self is now a culture’s ordinary product: a profile, a performance, a stream of positions. Merton’s claim is that this construction is not the person, and that the way past it is not a better performance. Unknowing, in his sense, is the undoing of the construction in the presence of a God who is not one of its materials. The later Merton adds that the undoing does not require a hatred of the city, the body, or the neighbor. That addition is what keeps the doctrine from becoming another costume of the false self, the costume of the person who has risen above the world.

The Wound of Knowledge reads the history of Christian spirituality, from the New Testament to John of the Cross, as a knowledge that arrives through the failure of the self’s projects. Spirituality, on this account, is not a technique for rising above suffering and the body. It is what happens to speech about God when a life is brought up against its limits. The mutation is from an ethic of attention to a Christology of attention.

Williams’s history says that the tradition’s greatest writers were people whose speech failed them in front of something, and that the failure was the knowledge. quote: We have to try to cure our faults by attention and not by will. […] Attention, taken to its highest degree, is the same thing as prayer.
author: Simone Weil
work: Gravity and Grace, “Attention and Will,” trans. Emma Craufurd (London: Routledge and Kegan Paul, 1952)
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. Weil’s central moral notion is attention. It is a negative effort, a waiting in which the greed of the self to seize, to explain, and to console itself is suspended so that a reality can appear. Affliction, malheur, is her name for a suffering that does not only hurt the body but destroys the person, the social and inward world that had made a life feel like a life. Decreation is the undoing of the imaginary self, so that what is created can pass through a human being without being confiscated by the ego. She treats the love of the order of the world and the love of the neighbor in affliction as one love. Plato’s Good beyond being, the Bhagavad Gita’s action without attachment, and the Christian mystics, John of the Cross especially, are the texts she makes speak to one another. The notebooks published after her death in 1943, edited into Gravity and Grace and Waiting for God, are where these notions were given to readers. They are not a system she finished.

The lineage she builds is itself a mutation. Platonic looking at the Good becomes an ethic of looking at a suffering person. The mystical night becomes a political fact about factory work, force, and the uprooting of peoples, themes of her essays on labor and of The Need for Roots. She is harder than the contemplative tradition on the question of force. The Iliad, in her reading, is a poem about force as the true hero, the thing that turns persons into things. Attention is the counter-practice: the refusal to let a person become a thing in one’s gaze.

Her heirs divide the inheritance. Iris Murdoch takes the moral psychology, unselfing and the just gaze, and sets it under Plato’s Good with far less of Weil’s theology of the void. Merton recognizes the kinship with contemplation and lives it inside a church she approached and never simply joined. Kingsnorth, Berry, and the critics of the Machine cite her on uprootedness and on attention as what a humane life requires. Each heir drops something. Murdoch drops the mystical metaphysics. The political readers sometimes drop the severity about the self. The notebooks hold both, which is why they remain difficult.

Copyright keeps her sentences out of this file. The ideas are stated here as ideas, and the books are the place where her wording does the work. What this set can say without those sentences is the connection. Her attention is the Cloud’s loving power, translated into an ethic that can stand in a factory and in front of an afflicted neighbor. Decreation is Eckhart’s poverty, translated into a psychology of the imaginary self. The translation is the twentieth century’s, and it is one of the ways the older pages still bite.

quote: Love is the perception of individuals. Love is the extremely difficult realisation that something other than oneself is real. Love, and so art and morals, is the discovery of reality.
author: Iris Murdoch
work: “The Sublime and the Good,” Chicago Review 13, no. 3 (Autumn 1959), p. 51
expansion: The extract is from the 1959 essay, and it is the claim the later book keeps. The Sovereignty of Good, three essays from the years around 1970, argues that the moral life is a life of attention and not a series of acts of will. The enemy is a picture she found both in the existentialism of her time and in the linguistic philosophy around her: a solitary will that chooses, in a naked moment, among values it has not been shaped by. She treats the ego as a greedy persistence. Goodness is its gradual defeat. Beauty is one of the ordinary places the defeat begins, because a beautiful thing draws attention off the self before the self has decided to be good. The Good itself she describes, with Plato, as a magnetic focus, real, not a person, and not a formula. An attentive, loving look at a particular reality, a face, a kestrel, a work of art, is what she means by the virtue of attention, and she says plainly that the notion comes from Simone Weil. Art, especially the realistic novel, matters because it trains that gaze. Fantasy, the ego’s self-soothing story, is the opposite of attention.

The lineage is Weil, Plato’s sun, and a refusal of Kant’s autonomous will as the last word about morality. She had written on Sartre and knew the Oxford moral philosophy of her colleagues. The essays are the break with both, in favor of a moral realism in which the Good is discovered by looking and not invented by choosing. The mutation from Weil is deliberate. Murdoch keeps decreation’s psychology, the undoing of the greedy self, and she is wary of Weil’s more extreme metaphysics of affliction and the void. She wants the world to remain, seen accurately and therefore loved. Unselfing is for the sake of the real, not for the sake of an escape from it.

Schopenhauer’s ethical sublime is a structural ancestor she does not need to claim. Knowledge holding its ground where the will would seize is his description and, in another vocabulary, hers. The difference is the destination. He is on the way to the denial of the will. She is on the way to a Good that justifies the endless effort of seeing. Keats’s claim that Beauty obliterates consideration is a Romantic cousin of her claim that beauty is an occasion of unselfing, with the difference that she trusts a long discipline of attention more than she trusts a poetic annihilation.

The essays are a criticism of a culture that has made sincerity and choice the whole of ethics. If the will is the only moral faculty, then a strong preference, authentically felt, is already a moral achievement. Murdoch thinks that is the ego congratulating itself. The counter-picture is slow, local, and perceptual. One learns to see a particular person who is not a function of one’s need. That is the same labor the ethical sublime described and the same labor Weil called attention, stated for a secular reader who still wants the Good to be more than a preference.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Bachelard’s career turns on a reversal. In the earlier epistemological books, of which The Psychoanalysis of Fire is the imaginative case, the image is an obstacle. Scientific thought has to psychoanalyze itself free of the dreams that cluster around fire, water, and the other elements, because those dreams distort the concepts. In the later books, The Poetics of Space and The Poetics of Reverie above all, the same images are no longer obstacles. Reverie is a primary mode of consciousness. It is not the nocturnal dream, which overwhelms the dreamer. It is a waking, valorizing imagination in which the dreamer is present and the image gives the world a value. He distinguishes a material imagination, which cleaves to the elements, from a formal imagination, which draws outlines. The elements are not metaphors one chooses. They are the materials in which imagination actually works, and each has its own cosmos of images.

The reversal is the thing to watch, because it is a mutation inside one mind. The philosopher of the epistemological break, close to a rationalist severity about what counts as knowledge, becomes the phenomenologist of the poetic image. He does not cancel the early work. He changes the status of what it had called an obstacle. The image is an obstacle for the concept and a truth for the imagination, and both descriptions can stand if one stops demanding that imagination justify itself before the sciences. That settlement is his gift to a Romantic tradition that had always trusted the image and had lacked a patient description of how an image holds a consciousness.

Novalis’s dream-room, Goethe’s insistence that a phenomenon carries its own theory, and Jung’s archetypal image are the neighborhood. Bachelard is cooler than Jung. He does not found a therapy, and he is wary of reducing the image to a hidden complex, which is what his own early ‘psychoanalysis’ of the elements risked. The later poetics lets the image be an origin. Hillman and the archetypal psychologists read him as an ally in the defense of the image against the concept. Corbin would add that a phenomenology of reverie is still a description of a subject, and that the imaginal world is not exhausted by the reverie that perceives it.

The present use is the rehabilitation of a kind of thinking that a technical culture classifies as mood. Reverie, in his late sense, is a way of knowing value. A house, a flame, a drawer, a shell, holds a consciousness and teaches it what intimacy, secrecy, and vastness are. The education of attention that runs through Weil, Murdoch, and the contemplatives has, in Bachelard, its poetic phenomenology. One learns the world by dreaming it well, awake.

quote: Now my aim is clear: I must show that the house is one of the greatest powers of integration for the thoughts, memories and dreams of mankind. The binding principle in this integration is the daydream.
author: Gaston Bachelard
work: The Poetics of Space, trans. Maria Jolas (Boston: Beacon Press, 1994; translation first published New York: Orion Press, 1964), p. 6
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. The Poetics of Space studies the house as a topography of intimacy. Rooms, cellars, attics, drawers, chests, nests, and shells are not illustrations of psychological facts one already has. They are the spaces in which intimacy, secrecy, and refuge are actually imagined, and therefore the spaces in which those experiences take on their form. The miniature, a thing small enough to be dominated by the gaze, and the vast, a thing large enough to overwhelm it, are two poles of the same imagination of space. He calls the method a phenomenology of the image: one receives the image in its suddenness, before the habits of criticism have reduced it to a cause. The house one was born in is, on this account, more than a scene of memory. It is a body of images that continues to organize how a later life feels shelter and exposure.

The book is the spatial case of the late Bachelard. Where the element books follow material imagination through fire and water, this one follows the imagination of inhabited space. Heidegger’s dwelling is the philosophical cousin, argued from the history of Being rather than from the poetic image. Bachelard does not need that history. He needs the poem and the daydream, and he reads them as modes in which space becomes human without becoming merely subjective. The nest and the shell matter because a living creature’s body and its house are imaginatively continuous. Interiority is something one builds and something one finds.

Berry’s household and the agrarian sense of place are a moral mutation of a theme Bachelard leaves phenomenological. The house, for Berry, is a membership of work, food, and the dead, and its destruction is a cultural wound. For Bachelard the destruction would be an amputation of images. Both are saying that an uprooted life is not only a life short of resources. It is a life short of the spaces in which the soul learns its scale. Weil’s uprootedness is the third name of the same loss, stated as a need of the person.

The book is a manual of attention for the inside of ordinary rooms. A culture that treats interior space as square footage, and memory as storage, has no use for the difference between a chest and a closet, or between an attic and a cellar. Bachelard’s claim is that those differences are differences of being. Learning to read them is part of the same education as learning to read a face or a landscape. The imaginal begins at home, in the drawer.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Neumann, a student and correspondent of Jung, reads myth as the phylogeny of consciousness. The Origins and History of Consciousness traces a path from the uroboros, the circling totality in which ego and unconscious are not yet distinguished, through the separation of the world parents, the hero’s fight, and the emergence of a center that can relate to the depths without being swallowed. Centroversion is his name for that striving of the psyche to become a center. The Great Mother then studies the archetype from which the hero separates, in its nourishing and its devouring aspects, across a wide field of images. The ego, on this map, is a late and precarious achievement. It is not the master of the house. It is the organ that has won enough freedom to enter a relationship with what it came out of.

work: The Origins and History of Consciousness (1949) and The Great Mother (1955); paraphrase, not a quotation
expansion: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Neumann, a student and correspondent of Jung, reads myth as the phylogeny of consciousness. The Origins and History of Consciousness traces a path from the uroboros, the circling totality in which ego and unconscious are not yet distinguished, through the separation of the world parents, the hero’s fight, and the emergence of a center that can relate to the depths without being swallowed. The scheme is a mutation of Jung’s archetypes into a history. Where Jung is wary of lining the archetypes up as stages everyone must pass, Neumann risks the sequence. The gain is a narrative of how an ego comes to be. The cost is a map that can be mistaken for a law, and that genders the law: consciousness as the hero’s separation from a maternal unconscious. Later criticism, including feminist criticism inside and outside analytical psychology, has pressed hard on that gendering. The pressure is part of the tradition’s honesty. A morphology of consciousness that cannot survive being asked whose body it has cast as the thing to be left behind has become an ideology.

Set beside Spengler, Neumann is doing a morphology of the soul rather than of cultures, and he owes the ambition to Jung’s reading of myth as psychic structure. Set beside Plotinus, the sequence is a psychology of the same hierarchy Plotinus described as levels of contemplation. The undifferentiated beginning, the emergence of a seeing center, the danger of falling back: III.8’s account of weak contemplation hurried into action is a metaphysical cousin of the ego that cannot yet hold the vision. Neumann tells it as a human drama of mothers, heroes, and births.

The use of the map is diagnostic, with the criticism kept in view. Inflations of the ego and collapses back into the mass are, on his terms, failures of centroversion. A culture of spectacle produces both, the performed self and the dissolved self, and calls them individuality. The Great Mother’s double face, the feeder and the devourer, is a warning against sentimentalizing the unconscious as a resource one can mine. Relationship is the achievement. Fusion and conquest are the two ways of missing it.

summary: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Neumann, a student and correspondent of Jung, reads myth as the phylogeny of consciousness. The Origins and History of Consciousness traces a path from the uroboros, the circling totality in which ego and unconscious are not yet distinguished, through the separation of the world parents, the hero’s fight, and the emergence of a center that can relate to the depths without being swallowed. Centroversion is his name for that striving of the psyche to become a center. The Great Mother then studies the archetype from which the hero separates, in its nourishing and its devouring aspects, across a wide field of images. The ego, on this map, is a late and precarious achievement. It is not the master of the house. It is the organ that has won enough freedom to enter a relationship with what it came out of.

quote: Fairy tales are the purest and simplest expression of collective unconscious psychic processes. Therefore their value for the scientific investigation of the unconscious exceeds that of all other material. They represent the archetypes in their simplest, barest, and most concise form.
author: Marie-Louise von Franz
work: The Interpretation of Fairy Tales, revised edition, chapter 1 (Boulder: Shambhala, 1996), p. 1
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. Von Franz, who worked with Jung from the 1930s and carried on his alchemical research after his death, treats the fairy tale as the purest and simplest expression of the collective unconscious. Myths, in her account, have already been worked over by a culture’s theology and history. The tale, passed from mouth to mouth, keeps the archetypal skeleton with less overlay. Interpretation is the art of letting that skeleton show, figure by figure, without forcing the story to illustrate a theory the interpreter brought in. She also continued the reading of alchemy as a symbolism of psychic transformation, the work Jung had opened in his late books. The laboratory operations, the vessels, the conjunctions, are images of a process in the soul, and the fairy tale is often the plainer telling of a process the alchemical texts tell in a learned code.

The lineage is Jung’s, and the mutation is a shift of emphasis toward the anonymous tale and toward the feminine figures the tales carry. Where Neumann builds a heroic sequence of the ego’s emergence, von Franz stays with the story as it is told, and the story frequently knows more than the hero does. That difference matters. A morphology that arranges myths into a progress of consciousness can miss the tale’s own irony, the youngest son, the animal helper, the girl who does not fight the witch by becoming a better warrior. Her work is the corrective inside the same school.

Bachelard’s elements and Corbin’s imaginal world are the neighboring defenses of the image. Von Franz is more willing than Corbin to let the image be a fact of the psyche, and more willing than Bachelard to let it be a fact of a collective psyche rather than of a single reverie. Hillman, Moore, and Bly all read in the space she helped clear, the space in which a folk tale is a serious text. Giegerich will later say that this whole space still literalizes soul as a gallery of images. Her answer is already in the method: the image is interpreted, not worshipped, and the interpretation is answerable to the tale.

The practice is a discipline of reading. A story is not a delivery system for a moral one already believes. Attention to the sequence, to who helps and who hinders and what is repeated three times, is a form of the same justice Murdoch asks of the gaze. For a reader drawn to the imaginal and suspicious of inspirational uses of myth, her standard is the right one. The tale is wiser than the paraphrase, including this one. The books are where the stories are actually read.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Giegerich, a Jungian analyst, argues that soul is logical life. It is the inwardness of thought thinking itself, not a place inside the person where images are stored and not a mythic land one visits. He thinks much archetypal psychology, Hillman’s included, still pictures the soul as a realm of figures, and that this picture literalizes what is actually a movement of meaning. When Jung in his late work said that the psyche thinks, Giegerich takes the sentence with Hegelian seriousness. The phenomenon, the symptom, the dream, wants to be thought through to its notion. Psychology’s task is to follow that self-movement, dialectically, until the image has been interiorized into the concept it was already trying to be. A psychology that stops at the image, and encourages the patient to live with the figure, has, on his account, refused the soul’s own next act.

Contemplation that is strong is the thing itself thinking. Giegerich’s ‘logical life’ is a modern, historical version of that rank-ordering, aimed at therapists. Eckhart’s letting-go of images is the mystical version. Giegerich would say the letting-go is not a mystical extra. It is what thinking is when it does not stop halfway.

The relevance for this set is the quarrel it forces. A love of Corbin, of fairy tales, of Blake, of the dream-room in Novalis, can settle into a connoisseurship of pictures. Giegerich’s question is whether the picture has been allowed to think. If the answer is only another picture, the soul, in his sense, has been refused. The books are difficult and polemical. They are the sharpest late correction inside the tradition they inherit.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Moore writes, from a background in a religious order and from a long reading of Hillman and of Marsilio Ficino, against a therapeutic culture whose aim is to cure the soul of its symptoms. Care, in the Renaissance sense he recovers from Ficino, is a tending, not a fixing. Depression, obsession, and the ordinary disorders of a household are the soul’s speech, and the work is to give them a worthy form rather than to silence them. The places of the work are ordinary: home, marriage, illness, a meal, a habit of beauty in daily things. He refuses both the clinic’s will to restore a functioning self and the fantasy that only a monastery is spiritual. Soul is the depth dimension of the life one is already in. The symptom is often the place where that dimension has been refused and is insisting.

The lineage is Ficino’s Book of Life, the Renaissance art of arranging music, images, and habits so that a melancholy temperament is cultivated rather than erased, and Hillman’s campaign against a psychology of development that wants the soul to grow up into a well-adapted ego. Moore is the popular mutation of that campaign, and the popularity has a cost. What in Hillman is a hard anti-humanist polemic becomes, in Care of the Soul, a counsel a general reader can use. The counsel is still serious when it remembers Ficino: beauty is a regimen, not a luxury. Music, color, and the arrangement of a day are medicines because the soul is imaginal before it is rational.

Set beside Merton, Moore is the affirmation of images inside a culture that has left the monastery. The false self, in Merton’s sense, is real, and Moore’s way with it is less ascetical. He would rather educate the symptom than starve the ego. Set beside Pieper’s leisure, which this file cannot quote, the kinship is the defense of uselessness. A life scheduled entirely for function has already decided against the soul. Care is the reintroduction of times and objects that do not pay.

The book is vulnerable to being read as comfort. Read as a descendant of Ficino and Hillman, it is a criticism. A culture that medicalizes every sadness and optimizes every hour has lost the distinction between a disease and a descent. Some descents are illnesses. Some are the soul asking for a form. The art Moore wants is the art of telling those apart without handing the second over to the techniques invented for the first.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Iron John reads a Grimm tale as a sequence of initiation. A wild man is found at the bottom of a pool, brought into a castle, and becomes the secret teacher of a boy who has stolen a key and fled. Ashes, a wound, a garden, a war, and a return are stations. Bly’s claim, argued as a poet who had come to fairy tales through Jung and through the same interpretive tradition as von Franz, is that a culture without ritual descent produces men who either inflate or collapse. The wildness the tale hides under the water is not a permission to be violent. It is a vitality that has to be met, disciplined, and brought back. The wound is part of the education. A manhood that has never gone down is, in the book’s sense, still a boy in a king’s house, handling objects whose power he has not suffered.
author: Robert Bly

The book became a public phenomenon and was criticized, fairly, when it hardened into a movement of weekend rites and a blame of mothers and of women. The criticism belongs in any honest account. Neumann’s map of the hero leaving the Great Mother is the Jungian scheme Bly’s popular version often slid toward, and the slide is the danger von Franz’s closer reading of tales resists. The tale itself is stranger and less ideological than the movement. Bly the poet, the author of Silence in the Snowy Fields, is closer to the tale than Bly the spokesman. The initiation claim, kept at that pitch, is the claim that matters: a psyche that never descends will counterfeit descent as depression, addiction, or a performed fierceness.

The older lineage is the ritual pattern the history of religions describes, Eliade’s initiation as a death and a return, here applied to a Grimm text and to a modern absence. Williams’s exchange and the contemplative tradition’s dark night are different descents, theological rather than masculine. They share the conviction that a transformation that does not pass through a loss is a change of costume. Bly’s contribution is to say that modern men, specifically, have been given no form for the loss, and have been told that the lack of a form is freedom.

Read now, after the reaction against the book, the usable part is the suspicion of a life that never goes under. Initiation is not a product and not a persona. It is a structured encounter with something in oneself that is not civilized yet and that will be destructive if it is only repressed or only indulged. The tale is the structure. The commentary is secondary, and at its worst it betrayed the tale. At its best it remembered that fairy stories are about the price of becoming a human being.

quote: Between them there is a world that is both intermediary and intermediate, described by our authors as the 'alam al-mithal, the world of the image, the mundus imaginalis: a world that is ontologically as real as the world of the senses and that of the intellect.
author: Henry Corbin
work: “Mundus Imaginalis, or the Imaginary and the Imaginal,” trans. Ruth Horine, Spring (Zürich, 1972); first published in Cahiers internationaux de symbolisme 6 (Brussels, 1964), pp. 3–26
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. Corbin, the scholar of Suhrawardi and Ibn Arabi, argues for a world that our languages keep collapsing into two others. The imaginary is the unreal, the merely made-up. The intelligible is the abstract concept. Between them, in the Islamic Platonism he spent his life reading, lies the imaginal world, alam al-mithal, a real order of being perceived by an organ of imagination that can be trained. There, symbols have bodies and bodies are symbols. Events of the soul are events of a world, not contents of a subject. The 1964 essay names this mundus imaginalis precisely in order to keep it from being translated as ‘imaginary.’ Creative Imagination in the Sufism of Ibn Arabi studies the organ itself, the heart as a power of perception, and theophany as the mode in which the divine shows itself in a form that is neither the divine essence nor a metaphor for it.

The polemic inside the claim is against the psychologizing of the symbol. Jung’s archetypes, which Corbin knew through the Eranos meetings, are the near temptation. A symbol taken as a fact of the human psyche has been captured by the subject. Corbin insists the imaginal is encountered. Hillman learned the word from him and built an archetypal psychology that Corbin’s distinction judges: if the figures are only ours, the mundus has been lost even while its vocabulary is kept. Giegerich then judges Hillman for stopping at the figures. The chain Corbin, Hillman, Giegerich is a real argument among people who shared a set of texts, and the first term of it is the refusal to let the imaginal collapse into the psyche.

Novalis’s dream that leads Hyacinth to the veiled maiden is a Romantic scene of the same ontology, written before the word. Dante’s journey, which Corbin read as a kin of the visionary recital, is the medieval Christian scene. Suhrawardi’s western exile and Ibn Arabi’s theophanic prayer are the sources. The mutation Corbin performs is to make the scene into a philosophical category aimed at modern habits of reading. Historicism reduces the vision to a document of its time. Allegory reduces it to a concept in fancy dress. The imaginal is his third term. The vision is an event in a real world, and the right reading is ta'wil, a leading of the phenomenon back to its origin, not a decoding.

For a reader who loves Blake, Novalis, fairy tales, and the Platonic tradition, this is the twentieth-century name of the love. It is also a warning. The love can be indulged as taste, a preference for beautiful images. Corbin’s claim is ontological or it is nothing. Either there is an organ and a world, or the word imaginal is a mood. The books and the essay are the argument. Nothing here replaces their wording.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Ta'wil, as Corbin explains it across his studies of Avicenna’s visionary recitals and of Ismaili hermeneutics, is a leading back. A text or an event is returned toward its origin, and the return is a spiritual act of the reader, who does not stand outside the text and translate it into a concept he already possessed. Allegory, in the sense he refuses, says: this image means that idea, and once the idea is had the image may be dropped. Ta'wil says: the image is the form in which a reality at another level of being becomes perceptible, and the reader’s own being is increased by perceiving it. Theophanic perception is the companion notion. What is truly seen is a face of the divine showing itself, not a sign pointing elsewhere. The seer and the seen are both implicated. A hermeneutic that leaves the reader unchanged has not performed ta'wil, whatever concepts it has extracted.

The sources are Quranic and philosophical: a tradition of commentary in which the literal sense is kept and is also the starting point of an ascent, Suhrawardi’s Oriental philosophy, and Avicenna’s recitals, which Corbin reads as initiations rather than as allegories of a finished Aristotelian system. The mutation he offers the modern West is a way to read visionary literature, Dante, the Romantic Märchen, Blake, without the two habits he thinks have captured the university. One habit is the historicist reduction. The other is the allegorical reduction. Both leave the reader the person he was. Ta'wil is a reading that requires an organ, the same organ the mundus imaginalis requires.

There is a tension with the negative theology elsewhere in this set, and it is fruitful. Dionysius and the Cloud unsay the images. Corbin’s tradition multiplies them, because the only way the One shows itself to a finite perceiver is in a form. Williams’s two ways are the Christian statement of the same tension. Ta'wil is the way of affirmation given a technical name and a textual practice. It does not cancel the apophatic warning. A form taken for the essence is the idolatry Barfield also named. The form taken as a theophany is the alternative.

The practice, for a reader, is a standard. If a commentary on a poem or a tale could be fully understood by someone who never returned to the poem, it was allegory in the sense Corbin disliked. If the commentary sends the reader back to the image with a larger capacity to see it, it was closer to ta'wil. That standard judges scholarship, and it judges the expansions in this file. They are guides. The texts are the place of the seeing.

quote: Origin is ever-present. It is not a beginning, since all beginning is linked with time.
author: Jean Gebser
work: The Ever-Present Origin, trans. Noel Barstad and Algis Mickunas (Athens: Ohio University Press, 1985), Preface, p. xxvii
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. Gebser describes consciousness as a series of mutations of structure, not as a progress of knowledge inside one structure. He names an archaic structure, a magical one, a mythical one, the mental structure that comes to dominance in Greece and in the modern West, and an integral structure that he thinks is now possible and not guaranteed. Each structure has an efficient form and a deficient form. The deficient mental is the late form of perspective and ratio: a consciousness that takes its own abstractions for the world, fragments what it looks at, and cannot see the structures it has superseded because it has defined reality as what its method can grasp. The integral mutation, as he hopes for it, is diaphany. The earlier structures become transparent. They are not abolished and not regressed into. Origin is ever-present, not located at the beginning of a timeline. A mutation is a change in the way time itself is lived.

He writes out of the crisis of the European mid-century, and Spengler is the predecessor he both uses and refuses. The morphological eye, the sense that a culture has a form of consciousness and not just a list of inventions, is Spengler’s gift. The death sentence, the claim that a culture is an organism that must die, is what Gebser drops. A structure can enter a deficient mode and still mutate. That is his difference, and it is why readers who have been educated by the Decline often find him a way to keep the diagnosis without the fatalism. He also wrote on the modern crisis in the arts and on Rilke, for whom the transparency of things was a poetic task. The integral, at its best, is a philosophical name for a transparency Rilke asked of saying.

Barfield’s original and final participation are the independent English cousin. Magical and mythical consciousness correspond, roughly, to a participated world. The mental structure corresponds to the withdrawal. Final participation corresponds to the integral, with the important difference that Barfield’s path runs through Coleridge, Goethe, and Steiner, and Gebser’s through a European phenomenology of civilizational form. Taylor’s buffered self is a finer-grained history of the mental structure’s social face. None of these men is a disciple of the others. The convergence is the reason for reading them together.

The deficient mental is a recognizable weather. Metrics, procedures, and viewpoints multiply, and the world thins. Gebser’s warning is that the remedy is not a return to myth, which in a mental age becomes a deficient myth, a costume. The remedy he points at is a consciousness in which myth, magic, and ratio are present and seen through. Whether that mutation is happening is a question he poses rather than a fact he proves. The book is the phenomenology of the question.

quote: To say that our desires are imitative or mimetic is to root them neither in their objects nor in ourselves but in a third party, the model or mediator, whose desire we imitate in the hope of resembling him or her.
author: René Girard
work: Resurrection from the Underground: Feodor Dostoevsky, trans. James G. Williams (New York: Crossroad, 1997), p. 144
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. Girard’s first claim is that desire is mimetic. We learn what to want from a model, and the model becomes a rival as soon as the wanting converges on an object that cannot be shared. The great novels, in Deceit, Desire and the Novel, are the texts that tell this truth against the romantic lie that desire is original, spontaneous, and one’s own. Cervantes, Stendhal, Flaubert, Proust, and Dostoevsky are his witnesses. The second claim, in Violence and the Sacred and The Scapegoat, is that a community in crisis discharges the rivalry onto a victim. The expulsion or the killing restores peace, and the peace is then told as a sacred story in which the victim is guilty and, often, later divine. Myth, on this reading, is the persecutor’s account. Biblical narrative, and the Gospels in particular, take the side of the victim and so begin to make the mechanism visible. He came to regard this unveiling as the reason for his own conversion to Christianity.

The argument is a rival theory of the sacred, and the rivals are inside this set. Eliade’s sacred is a manifestation, a break in the homogeneity of space and time. Corbin’s sacred is a theophany in the imaginal world. Girard’s sacred is a violence that has been hidden by the story the beneficiaries tell. A reader who loves myth has to let the three stand in the same room. The love is not refuted by Girard. It is put under a question: whose body is the unity of the group purchased with? Nietzsche is the modern philosopher he argues with most directly, because Nietzsche saw the victimary mechanism with extraordinary clarity and, in Girard’s judgment, took the side of the persecutors.

The mutation across his own books is from literary criticism to a theory of culture and then to a theology. Each step is contested, by classicists, by anthropologists, and by theologians who think he has thinned the Gospel to a piece of information about violence. The contest is part of the inheritance. Attention, in Weil’s and Murdoch’s sense, is the local antidote: a gaze that lets a person be real enough that they cannot serve as a function of one’s desire or as the cause of one’s peace. quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. The Gnostic Religion describes a syndrome. In the texts of late antique gnosis, the world is a prison made by lesser powers, the true self is a spark from beyond, and salvation is the remembering of an alien origin. Jonas argues that this is a dualism hostile to the cosmos, and that modern nihilism, after the death of a meaningful cosmic order, repeats the syndrome without the myth: a self for whom the universe is indifferent, and a contempt for nature dressed as honesty. He had been Heidegger’s student, and he came to think that existentialism shared the gnostic refusal of the world. The Imperative of Responsibility is the late mutation of the diagnosis. Technological action now reaches far beyond the actor’s lifetime and beyond the actor’s power to undo. Ethics has to answer for the future of vulnerable life. Nature is no longer the stage on which a self seeks its authenticity. It is the object of a duty, and the duty runs to generations who cannot consent.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. The Experience of God argues that God, in the classical tradition shared by Christian, Jewish, Muslim, Hindu, and Platonic thought, is not a being among beings and not a cause inside the system of causes. God is the infinite actuality in which any finite thing exists at all: being, consciousness, and bliss as the names of that actuality, not as three qualities added to a large invisible person. A debate that treats theism as the hypothesis that one more object exists somewhere has, on this account, changed the subject. The Beauty of the Infinite, his earlier and more technical book, argues against a metaphysics that treats difference as inevitably violent. Beauty is the showing of a peaceful difference, a rhetoric of peace, and Christian theology’s persuasive form is closer to that showing than to a system that has secured itself against every rival. Glory is not an ornament on doctrine. It is how the infinite is known by a finite mind.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Beauty, as Scruton defends it, is a reason. A face, a building, a melody, a stretch of country addresses a person and asks to be contemplated for its own sake. The experience is not a private pleasure one happens to have, and it is not a political instrument. It carries a summons: attend, and in attending become answerable to the thing. Much of what a century of criticism has said against beauty, that it is bourgeois, that it is a mask of power, that it is mere preference, he treats as a refusal of that summons. The Soul of the World extends the claim into a metaphysics of the sacred. Persons, home, and the edge of death disclose a world that looks back. The scientific image of objects in a causal field is real and incomplete. The world has a soul in the sense that it can be addressed and can address, and a culture that has lost the second-person relation to reality has lost the sacred even if it has kept the explanations.

quote: A healthy farm culture can be based only upon familiarity and can grow only among a people soundly established upon the land; it nourishes and safeguards a human intelligence of the earth that no amount of technology can satisfactorily replace.
author: Wendell Berry
work: The Unsettling of America: Culture and Agriculture (San Francisco: Sierra Club, 1986; first published 1977), p. 43
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. The Unsettling of America describes a mind, the industrial mind, that treats land and body as raw material and calls the treatment progress. Against it Berry sets membership. A household, a farm, a small town, when they are working, are a single pattern of work, eating, care of the dead, and knowledge of a particular place. Fidelity to that place is an epistemology. One knows by staying, by suffering the consequences of one’s methods in the same soil one will hand on. Abstraction, the knowledge that can be applied anywhere because it is responsible nowhere, is the intellectual form of the unsettlement. He writes as a farmer and as a Christian, and the essays return to the same joint: a culture’s health is visible in how it eats, how it works, and whether its language can still tell the truth about both.

The lineage he claims is less German metaphysics than a biblical care for the given, joined to an argument with the American tradition of the independent farm. Jefferson’s yeoman is in the background and is criticized where the yeoman becomes a figure of expansion. The nearer modern kin are the ones who saw technique as a spiritual form. Weil on uprootedness, Ellul on technique, and later Kingsnorth on the Machine, who names Berry as a predecessor, are the company. Goethe’s delicate empiricism is an unclaimed cousin: a knowing that stays with the phenomenon and will not trade it for a grid. Berry’s version is agricultural and moral. The grid is what lets a field become a quantity.

Spengler’s megalopolis, the late city that has replaced destiny with calculation, is the diagnosis Berry lives downstream of without needing the morphology. Taylor’s immanent frame is the felt world in which Berry’s neighbors are asked to believe that a place is a site. Crawford’s skilled work is the defense of the hand that Berry makes for the farm. They converge on a refusal of the bargain Wilhelm Meister’s burgher was offered, usefulness bought by the amputation of every power but one.

The essays are a standard for a love of landscape that might otherwise stay aesthetic. A beautiful place that no one is answerable for is already an image. Membership is the answerability. It is also the form, in an American voice, of the rootedness Weil thought a soul needs in order to attend. Attention, in Berry, is local or it is a mood. The books and the poems are the practice of a speech that has agreed to be local.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Pilgrim at Tinker Creek is a book of seeing, written from a year beside a creek in Virginia. Dillard distinguishes a kind of looking that searches, active and directed, from a kind of waiting in which something is given to a gaze that has stopped hunting. Both are disciplines. What they find is extravagant and violent as well as beautiful. The creek’s abundance, the insects, the waste, the particular cruelty of the natural world, are not edited into a lesson about harmony. Glory and cost arrive together, and the moral pressure of the book is to stay with what is actually there long enough that wonder becomes a perception rather than a mood one brought to the water. Seeing is compared, at times, to a stalking. It is also compared to a letting-go. The prose is the record of a person training both.

Her difference is the refusal of a tidy transcendental consolation. The world she watches will not reliably symbolize a moral order. It will, if attended to, overwhelm the observer with a presence that feels charged, and the charge includes the parasitic and the predatory. She keeps it nailed to the thing in front of her, so that the image does not float free of the water.

quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Kingsley argues that Parmenides, usually taught as the father of a logical ontology, was a priest of Apollo connected with incubation, the practice of lying down in darkness for a healing or oracular sleep. The prologue of the poem, the journey to the goddess, is on this reading the record of a practice, not a literary frame wrapped around a theory of being. The West’s rational tradition, he claims, begins in a mystical discipline it then forgot, and the forgetting is so successful that the poem is now read as the opposite of what it was. Reality presses the claim further, into a general account of how a civilization of the surface lost the underworld journey that had been its source of knowledge. The books are written for a general reader and are also dense with ancient evidence, archaeological and textual, about the south of Italy and the figure of the healer-priest.

Corbin’s visionary recitals are a later, Islamic form of a journey to a revealer. Kingsley is saying the Greek origin was already that kind of journey.

If the poem is an initiation, then the history of metaphysics begins in a ritual of the dark, and the separation of mysticism from philosophy is a later wound. quote: Hence, instead of defining man as an animal rationale, we should define him as an animal symbolicum.
author: Ernst Cassirer
work: An Essay on Man (New Haven: Yale University Press, 1944), p. 26
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. Cassirer’s philosophy of symbolic forms holds that myth, language, art, and science are not attempts, some failed and one successful, to copy a world that is already there. Each is a way of building a world. Man, in the formula of An Essay on Man, is the animal symbolicum. Myth is not bad science and not a childish science. It has its own principle of formation, its own way of configuring space, time, number, and the self. The task of a philosophy of culture is to understand these forms from the inside, as achievements of spirit, and to see how they generate the objects they then seem to find. The three volumes of The Philosophy of Symbolic Forms work the claim out for language, for mythical thought, and for the phenomenology of knowledge. The late Essay on Man is the shorter map.

author: Rainer Maria Rilke
work: Duineser Elegien, „Die neunte Elegie“, Leipzig: Insel-Verlag, 1923, S. 34
expansion: The extract is the German of the Ninth Elegy. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. The Duino Elegies ask what a human being is for, in a world where the animal seems at home and the angel seems terrible and remote. The Ninth Elegy turns the answer toward the earth. Things, the poem’s argument goes, want to be said. Saying is a transformation, not a description. What is visible is taken up into an inwardness and, in that sense, survives. The poet’s work is this work of transformation, and it is urgent because the earth needs it from us. The elegies do not hand the task to a church. They spend a Romantic inheritance, night and angel and a high unattainable beloved, on the praise of the perishable. Letters to a Young Poet, published in German in 1929 from letters written decades earlier, gives the accompanying ethic of a vocation: solitude, patience, the refusal to live by other people’s questions, and the counsel to live the questions themselves until one lives into an answer.

Novalis’s night is the ancestor the elegies both continue and spend differently. The hymn gives the night a sovereignty over the busy day. Rilke keeps a darkness and an angel and aims them at the saying of earthly things. The mutation is from a metaphysical night to an aesthetic of transience. Hölderlin’s sense of the poet’s task in a needy time is the other German ancestor, and Heidegger’s 1946 lecture on Rilke, ‘What Are Poets For?’, is the philosophical mutation of the elegies into a history of Being in a destitute age. That lecture should be read as Heidegger’s use of Rilke, not as Rilke’s own metaphysics. The poems remain poems of praise and of the difficulty of praise.

The Letters are the prose ethic that a century of readers has used as a manual of artistic seriousness. Their danger is the danger of any manual. Solitude and the lived question can become a style of postponement. Read beside the Ninth Elegy, they are stricter. The solitude is for the sake of a work that the earth, in the poem’s fiction, is waiting for. Goethe’s demand that the senses are how nature speaks, and Bachelard’s reverie on things, are the gentler cousins of this urgency. Rilke’s version hurts more, because the things are perishing and the saying is the only shelter he is willing to claim for them.

What can be said in prose is the claim the Ninth Elegy makes on a reader who loves things, landscapes, and works of art. Praise is a form of knowledge. It changes the one who praises and, in the poem’s sense, changes the status of the thing. A culture that only uses, catalogs, and displays has refused the transformation. The elegies are the demand that it be accepted.

author: T. S. Eliot
work: “Burnt Norton,” Four Quartets, in The Complete Poems and Plays, 1909–1950 (New York: Harcourt, Brace and Company, 1952), p. 119
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. Four Quartets takes the problem of time that ‘Tradition and the Individual Talent’ had stated as a critical doctrine and tries to live it. A moment in a rose garden, a wartime watch, a chapel at Little Gidding, each becomes a place where a life is answerable to more than succession. The poems refuse two escapes. One is the flight out of time into a timeless absolute that cancels history. The other is the reduction of meaning to historical process, as if the present were only the latest fact. What they circle is a stillness that is inside movement, and an Incarnation, in the Christian sense Eliot had accepted in 1927, as the place where the timeless and the temporal meet. The later quartets correct the early essay’s coldness about personality. Impersonality returns as humility, and as the acceptance of a life that cannot be made significant by the will alone. Dante, the Bhagavad Gita, and the English contemplative tradition, John of the Cross echoed rather than explained, are inside the sequence. Little Gidding the place is Nicholas Ferrar’s community, a historical prayer inside a poem about history.

The lineage from the 1919 essay is the one to keep clear. There, tradition is an ideal order of works, altered by the new work, and the poet escapes personality by joining it. Here, the order is metaphysical and biographical. A person’s own past, the lives of the dead in a place, and the moment of Incarnation are the simultaneity the historical sense had named. The mutation is from a theory of criticism to a religious poem, and it costs the theory its pride. The essay thinks the poet can obtain the tradition by great labor. The poems know long labor, and they also know that the significant moment is given.

Augustine’s account of time in the Confessions, the distention of the soul across past and future and the intention that gathers it, is the Latin ancestor of the poems’ difficulty with time. The Gita’s action without attachment is openly in the sequence’s background. The Cloud’s unknowing and John of the Cross’s night are the contemplative ancestors of the darkness the poems are willing to sit in. Eliot’s difference from the mystics is that he remains a poet of places and of a war. The unknowing happens in a garden, on a coast, in a chapel, during a fire watch. History is not left behind. It is the material of the intersection.

The sequence is the twentieth century’s English poem of the claim this whole collection is built on: that time is real, that more than time is real, and that the place they meet is the place a life is judged. A culture of the perpetual present, and a culture of nostalgia, are the two escapes the poems refuse. The first has no pastness. The second has no presence. The historical sense, lived rather than professed, is the holding of both. The poems are under copyright, and their lines are not reproduced here. The argument is the argument of the sequence, and the sequence is the text.

Truth, in the book’s central argument, is antinomic. The law of identity, the A that is only A, is the form of a dead self-sameness. A living truth holds contradictories together without collapsing into nonsense, and the Trinity is the pattern of that holding: identity that is also relation. The Russian lineage runs through Solovyov’s Godmanhood and a recovery of the Philokalia’s theology of the heart, joined to a mathematical mind that had learned both the precision and the paradoxes of modern logic. Bulgakov inherits the sophiological problem from Solovyov and from Florensky and changes it into a cosmology of Sophia. Florensky’s own emphasis is epistemological and personal. Florensky, a priest of the Orthodox Church, does not want a God who has been freed of the Trinity’s relations. The antinomy is the Trinity’s life, not a problem to be solved on the way to a simple One. That is his difference from a Platonism of the undifferentiated, and it is why Proclus’s One and Florensky’s truth should be read as a tension and not as a slogan.

It is answerable to dogma, to mathematics, and to the friend the letters are written to. A contradiction one has not suffered is not yet an antinomy. Florensky’s antinomy is the epistemological twin: a truth that holds contradictories. Bulgakov wants the contradictories of God and world to be held in a wisdom that is the world’s own depth. quote: Paraphrase, not a quotation. Kingsnorth uses the Machine as a name for a way of seeing, not for a collection of devices. It is the long project, from the industrial revolution through the present systems of computation and control, by which a living world is converted into resource, process, and standing reserve, and by which human beings are reshaped to match. Progress is the project’s moral language. Against the Machine, published in 2025 as the gathering of three decades of this argument, treats the project as a spiritual form. What it hollows out is attention, place, memory, and the capacity to regard anything as sacred. The essays that led to the book, many of them written in public as the Abbey of Misrule, track the same claim through culture and through his own movement from ecological despair toward Christianity. The remedy he points at is not a better device. It is a recovery of roots in place, in work, and in a discipline of the spirit that can tell the Machine no.

quote: A crucial condition for this was a new sense of the self and its place in the cosmos: not open and porous and vulnerable to a world of spirits and powers, but what I want to call “buffered”.
author: Charles Taylor
work: A Secular Age (Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 2007), p. 27
expansion: The extract is the author's wording. The rest of this note is a paraphrase of the argument around it. A Secular Age describes a change in the background of experience, not only a change in beliefs. A porous self, the self of an earlier age, is open. Meanings, spirits, and powers cross the boundary of the mind. A buffered self is its own interior. The world it meets is a mechanism, and the meanings are things it has, inside, as beliefs or feelings. The immanent frame is the sensed shape of a life in which the good is sought inside a self-sufficient natural order. Disenchantment is that shape, felt, before it is a theory. Secularity, in the sense he most wants, is the condition in which religious belief is one option among others, and in which the option of unbelief is the one that feels like the default. Sources of the Self, the earlier book, maps the moral sources of this inwardness, from Augustine’s turn inward, through the Reformation’s affirmation of ordinary life, to the modern esteem for the voice of nature and the voice of the self.

Weber’s disenchantment is the thesis he historicizes and complicates. The subtraction story, in which science simply removes superstition and leaves the real, is the story he rejects. The buffered self is an achievement, built by disciplines of reform, civility, and self-control, and it exacts a price. Barfield’s withdrawal of participation is the same event described from the side of perception and language. Taylor describes it from the side of moral experience and of the felt possibility of belief. Gebser’s mental structure is the civilizational name. They do not derive from one another. Together they are the best modern description of the world in which the older texts of this collection now have to be read.

The price, as he tells it, is not only the loss of spirits. It is a malaise: a flattening of time, a fragility of meaning, a self that has to generate its own significance inside a frame that does not support it. Romanticism, in his account, is one of the great attempts to recover a resonance the frame had muffled, sometimes by going deeper into the self, sometimes by finding it in nature. Goethe, Novalis, and the sacramental sense Berry and Dillard practice are, in this history, responses to a loss Taylor thinks is real and not merely nostalgic.

The books are long because the claim is historical. A mood of disenchantment that knows no history will either pretend the world was always a mechanism or pretend it can be re-enchanted by a decision. Taylor’s usefulness is the detail. The frame was built. It can be understood. Lives inside it still look for resonance, and the looking is not a failure of nerve. It is the sign that the buffered self has not exhausted what a person is. For a reader of this set, the two books are the map of the country the mystics, the Romantics, and their heirs are walking in.
